sources.title: TikTok “Permanently Suspends” the ‘Musk’ Film Ad Account, Raising Suppression Fears (Exclusive) - The Hollywood Reporter
passages: TikTok has banned the Musk film advertising account, citing a repeated pattern of political content that violates its policies.

The move, which comes just as the Alex Gibney ’s investigation into Elon Musk expands to more than 470 screens across North America, raises concerns about Big Tech suppression that the very film seeks to expose.
Distributor Bleecker Street was informed Friday afternoon a “permanent suspension” was coming regarding any ads it tried to buy, and the company was unable to do so shortly after.

The native unpaid TikTok account, which generally allows more leeway on so-called political content, remains active, though Bleecker Street is not allowed to pay to boost its content, as many companies traditionally do.
Musk goes deep on a number of its subject’s actions and companies, which Gibney spent more than three years investigating.
It also centers on his acquisition of Twitter, which Gibney suggests was done to control the digital public square, adding an element of irony to the TikTok move.
The former was piece of material was visible on the unpaid account, and had garnered 270,000 views.

TikTok has no official affiliation with Elon Musk, though it is partly owned by Larry Ellison, who gets a rough moment in the doc when a text from him offering to pay billions to the mogul to help finance his Twitter acquisition is shown.

TikTok has been more resistant to Musk content than some of its competitors, refusing to reverse its position against accepting an ad for the trailer even after Meta and Google/YouTube did just that .
Larry’s son David is set to release Gibney’s doc when his newly acquired HBO, which financed the film, puts in on the platform in 2027.
A spokesperson for the distributor confirmed that TikTok reps had informed them of the suspension and noted “disappointment” in the timing.
After grossing $70,000 in four theaters in New York and Los Angeles in its first weekend of release, Musk is now playing in dozens of cities this weekend.

The spokesperson said the company is in the process of appealing the move; even a reversal, however, could still prove costly if it doesn’t come during a weekend window when many people are likely to see the film.

Email correspondence between TikTok and Bleecker Street representatives shows a cycle of rejection and appeals on various paid posts, including the trailer, which an official said will “continue to get pulled from the platform” due to political content. sources.title: TikTok permanently bans ‘Musk’ documentary advertising account
passages: A four-hour documentary about Elon Musk continues to meet resistance from social media platforms, with TikTok banning the film’s advertising account.

According to a story in The Hollywood Reporter , the documentary’s distributor Bleecker Street was recently notified by TikTok that the account had received a “permanent suspension” due to its political content.
TechCrunch has reached out to TikTok for comment.
X, which Musk owns, has refused to carry ads for “Musk.” TikTok’s U.S. operations are partly owned by Larry Ellison — who, like Musk, has been a notable supporter of President Donald Trump.
“Musk” opened in just four theaters last weekend and is now rolling out more broadly.
Next year, it’s supposed to stream on HBO — now part of Paramount/Skydance and led by Ellison’s son David .

sources.title: TikTok permanently bans ‘Musk’ documentary advertising account
passages: A four-hour documentary about Elon Musk continues to meet resistance from social media platforms, with TikTok banning the film’s advertising account.

According to a story in The Hollywood Reporter , the documentary’s distributor Bleecker Street was recently notified by TikTok that the account had received a “permanent suspension” due to its political content.
TechCrunch has reached out to TikTok for comment.
X, which Musk owns, has refused to carry ads for “Musk.” TikTok’s U.S. operations are partly owned by Larry Ellison — who, like Musk, has been a notable supporter of President Donald Trump.
“Musk” opened in just four theaters last weekend and is now rolling out more broadly.
Next year, it’s supposed to stream on HBO — now part of Paramount/Skydance and led by Ellison’s son David .

passages: Meta recently updated its commercial terms of use, declaring that the company can “use any content from [a business account’s] domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta products and services.

According to legal experts interviewed by Nieman Lab , this looked like a “remarkable provision” that could give Meta permission to scrape the website of any publisher with a Meta business account and use the content to train the company’s AI models. (While Meta defeated a high-profile lawsuit over alleged copyright infringement last year, other cases against AI companies, including Meta, continue.)
“It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers.”
However, a Meta spokesperson insisted that the updated terms did not reflect a change in the way Meta crawls the web.
And now, The Verge reports that the provision has been removed.

passages: ISTANBUL (AA) - Meta has revised its commercial terms to remove language that raised concerns about the potential use of news websites to train artificial intelligence models.

Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts said the changes do not alter the company's existing crawling practices and that website owners can continue using robots.txt instructions to indicate their access preferences.
The provisions still allow Meta to use automated tools, including web scrapers, bots and crawlers, to access and collect content from websites associated with businesses using its platforms.
Meta subsequently removed the reference and clarified that the crawling provisions apply to advertising and business products.

extraction.body: Company removes training language from web-crawling provision, clarifies its use for advertising and business products ISTANBUL (AA) - Meta has revised its commercial terms to remove language that raised concerns about the potential use of news websites to train artificial intelligence models. The revised terms, scheduled to take effect on Oct. 30, specify that automated website crawling is intended to develop, improve, research and maintain advertising and business products. The provisions still allow Meta to use automated tools, including web scrapers, bots and crawlers, to access and collect content from websites associated with businesses using its platforms. An earlier version of the proposed terms included language about using collected material to "train" Meta products, prompting concerns among publishers and legal experts over the potential use of copyrighted news content for AI development. Meta subsequently removed the reference and clarified that the crawling provisions apply to advertising and business products. Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts said the changes do not alter the company's existing crawling practices and that website owners can continue using robots.txt instructions to indicate their access preferences. Meta Vice President of Communications Andy Stone also rejected suggestions that the update was intended to enable scraping of news websites, saying it was designed to retrieve accurate product information for advertising and content recommendations.

sources.title: Meta Scrubs AI Training Language After Privacy Backlash
passages: Meta's quiet retreat on AI training language reveals how sensitive the data rights question has become in the race to build next-generation AI.

The social media giant removed text that appeared to give it broad rights to scrape external websites for AI training data, though a company spokesperson insists nothing actually changed in how Meta crawls the web.

The removal of the controversial language might calm immediate concerns, but it doesn't answer the fundamental question: What data is Meta actually using to train its AI models, and where does it come from?
If the terms language was always meant to describe existing practices, the backlash suggests Meta failed to communicate clearly what those practices actually are.
And if the language accidentally revealed plans Meta wasn't ready to announce, removing it without explanation only deepens suspicion.
This isn't Meta's first rodeo with privacy concerns.
But if nothing changed, why remove the language at all?
The web scraping question cuts deeper than Meta's own ecosystem.

extraction.body: The social media giant removed text that appeared to give it broad rights to scrape external websites for AI training data, though a company spokesperson insists nothing actually changed in how Meta crawls the web. The reversal comes just days after legal experts confirmed the company's updated terms meant business account holders were consenting to AI training, adding fuel to an already raging debate about data rights in the AI era. The controversial text suggested Meta might be claiming rights to scrape content across the broader web to feed its AI models, not just data from its own platforms like Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp. For an industry already on edge about how tech giants are hoovering up training data, it was gasoline on a fire. "The updated terms did not reflect a change in the way Meta crawls the web," a Meta spokesperson told TechCrunch. But if nothing changed, why remove the language at all? The company hasn't elaborated, leaving the industry to read between the lines. Just this week, the company was caught in another data rights controversy when legal experts confirmed its updated terms meant business account holders were automatically consenting to AI training. That revelation sent small business owners and content creators scrambling to understand what data they'd inadvertently signed over. The web scraping question cuts deeper than Meta's own ecosystem. Meta has been racing to catch up in the AI arms race. The company recently introduced tools that let users control Facebook's algorithm using natural language, and it's betting big on AI-powered features across its product line. But every AI model needs training data, and lots of it. The question of where that data comes from and who consents to its use has become one of the most contentious issues in tech. The company's vague explanation isn't helping its case. If the terms language was always meant to describe existing practices, the backlash suggests Meta failed to communicate clearly what those practices actually are. And if the language accidentally revealed plans Meta wasn't ready to announce, removing it without explanation only deepens suspicion. Google has faced similar accusations about using web content for AI training, while OpenAI has struck licensing deals with publishers to avoid exactly this kind of controversy. The legal landscape remains murky, with courts still working out whether scraping publicly available data for AI training constitutes fair use. If AI models can ingest their content without permission or payment, what's their business model? The company needs massive amounts of data to compete with OpenAI and Google in generative AI, but it can't afford to alienate the businesses and creators that make its platforms valuable in the first place. The removal of the controversial language might calm immediate concerns, but it doesn't answer the fundamental question: What data is Meta actually using to train its AI models, and where does it come from? Until the company offers more transparency, expect the scrutiny to continue. This isn't Meta's first rodeo with privacy concerns. The company has spent years rebuilding trust after the Cambridge Analytica scandal and other data mishaps. Users and businesses are more sophisticated about data rights now, and they're not afraid to push back when terms seem overreaching. Meta's quiet retreat on AI training language reveals how sensitive the data rights question has become in the race to build next-generation AI. The company's insistence that nothing changed in its actual practices raises more questions than it answers, especially coming on the heels of the business account opt-in controversy. As tech giants compete for training data, expect more flashpoints like this. The companies that figure out transparent, fair data practices will have a strategic advantage, while those that stumble through vague terms and forced opt-ins risk regulatory crackdowns and user exodus.

coreStoryFacts.text: Meta recently updated its commercial terms of use, declaring that the company can “use any content from [a business account’s] domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta products and services.

According to legal experts interviewed by Nieman Lab , this looked like a “remarkable provision” that could give Meta permission to scrape the website of any publisher with a Meta business account and use the content to train the company’s AI models. (While Meta defeated a high-profile lawsuit over alleged copyright infringement last year, other cases against AI companies, including Meta, continue.)
“It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers.”
However, a Meta spokesperson insisted that the updated terms did not reflect a change in the way Meta crawls the web.
And now, The Verge reports that the provision has been removed.
ISTANBUL (AA) - Meta has revised its commercial terms to remove language that raised concerns about the potential use of news websites to train artificial intelligence models.

Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts said the changes do not alter the company's existing crawling practices and that website owners can continue using robots.txt instructions to indicate their access preferences.
The provisions still allow Meta to use automated tools, including web scrapers, bots and crawlers, to access and collect content from websites associated with businesses using its platforms.
Meta subsequently removed the reference and clarified that the crawling provisions apply to advertising and business products.
Meta's quiet retreat on AI training language reveals how sensitive the data rights question has become in the race to build next-generation AI.

The social media giant removed text that appeared to give it broad rights to scrape external websites for AI training data, though a company spokesperson insists nothing actually changed in how Meta crawls the web.

The removal of the controversial language might calm immediate concerns, but it doesn't answer the fundamental question: What data is Meta actually using to train its AI models, and where does it come from?
If the terms language was always meant to describe existing practices, the backlash suggests Meta failed to communicate clearly what those practices actually are.
And if the language accidentally revealed plans Meta wasn't ready to announce, removing it without explanation only deepens suspicion.
This isn't Meta's first rodeo with privacy concerns.

The controversial text suggested Meta might be claiming rights to scrape content across the broader web to feed its AI models, not just data from its own platforms like Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp.
For an industry already on edge about how tech giants are hoovering up training data, it was gasoline on a fire.
"The updated terms did not reflect a change in the way Meta crawls the web," a Meta spokesperson told TechCrunch.
But if nothing changed, why remove the language at all?
The company hasn't elaborated, leaving the industry to read between the lines.
Just this week, the company was caught in another data rights controversy when legal experts confirmed its updated terms meant business account holders were automatically consenting to AI training.
That revelation sent small business owners and content creators scrambling to understand what data they'd inadvertently signed over.
The web scraping question cuts deeper than Meta's own ecosystem.
Meta has been racing to catch up in the AI arms race.
The company recently introduced tools that let users control Facebook's algorithm using natural language, and it's betting big on AI-powered features across its product line.
But every AI model needs training data, and lots of it.
The question of where that data comes from and who consents to its use has become one of the most contentious issues in tech.
The company's vague explanation isn't helping its case.
If the terms language was always meant to describe existing practices, the backlash suggests Meta failed to communicate clearly what those practices actually are.
And if the language accidentally revealed plans Meta wasn't ready to announce, removing it without explanation only deepens suspicion.
Google has faced similar accusations about using web content for AI training, while OpenAI has struck licensing deals with publishers to avoid exactly this kind of controversy.
The legal landscape remains murky, with courts still working out whether scraping publicly available data for AI training constitutes fair use.
If AI models can ingest their content without permission or payment, what's their business model?

The company needs massive amounts of data to compete with OpenAI and Google in generative AI, but it can't afford to alienate the businesses and creators that make its platforms valuable in the first place.

The removal of the controversial language might calm immediate concerns, but it doesn't answer the fundamental question: What data is Meta actually using to train its AI models, and where does it come from?
Until the company offers more transparency, expect the scrutiny to continue.
This isn't Meta's first rodeo with privacy concerns.
The company has spent years rebuilding trust after the Cambridge Analytica scandal and other data mishaps.
Users and businesses are more sophisticated about data rights now, and they're not afraid to push back when terms seem overreaching.
Meta's quiet retreat on AI training language reveals how sensitive the data rights question has become in the race to build next-generation AI.
The company's insistence that nothing changed in its actual practices raises more questions than it answers, especially coming on the heels of the business account opt-in controversy.
As tech giants compete for training data, expect more flashpoints like this.

The companies that figure out transparent, fair data practices will have a strategic advantage, while those that stumble through vague terms and forced opt-ins risk regulatory crackdowns and user exodus.

extraction.body: As the tech industry continues to scale AI use, some companies are hitting snags not in the technology itself, but in the human workforce developing and working alongside AI agents. Fiona Fung, the engineering leader of Anthropic's Claude Code and Cowork teams, said in a recent episode of Lenny's Podcast that agentic AI use in the workplace has increased so much it was making employees' work more solitary, pushing the company to intervene with other team-building activities. "The other thing that we found interesting on the Claude Code team is, after a while, we felt it could start being a lonely experience because we all started just working with our agents so much," she said. Anthropic began implementing hackathons "just to make sure we're interacting together as a team," as well as pair programming lunches for employees to share how they're using Claude Code, Fung said. She deemed both interventions successful. "When we do pairwise programming, we actually learn so much from each other," she said. "Every time I watch someone work, I learn something myself as well." An Anthropic spokesperson said the company is paying close attention to how its AI tools impact how employees work together. "We're seeing engineers find new ways to learn from and build alongside one another, in what's really an evolution of pair programming," the spokesperson said in a statement to Fortune . "Where pairing was once about working through a tough problem together, it's now increasingly about seeing how a colleague uses these new tools and systems differently than you might, so even as more of the work shifts toward collaborating with agents, engineers keep learning from one another. Sharing how our own work is changing, including the hard parts, helps us build tools that best serve the people using them." While Anthropic leaders like Fung said the company has adapted to challenges tech employees have faced as they increase AI use, the loneliness some tech employees are facing may shed light on a larger morale issue in a rapidly changing industry. There have been about 120,000 tech layoffs in 2026 so far, nearly equaling 2025's total. Some of the companies driving the layoffs, including Meta , which let go of 8,000 workers this year, have cited AI as the reason behind the reductions. Many tech employees left unscathed by layoffs are still reeling from changes to their work, as well as the anxiety these reductions and AI advancements bring. On the social media site Blind, a platform where verified anonymous users can discuss their workplaces, tech workers lamented low morale following layoff announcements and geopolitical uncertainty, as well as a changing culture of employees becoming less critical of leadership, which they link to risks of less innovation. "The whole mood has changed," Sunguk Moon, cofounder and CEO of Blind, told the New York Times last month. "It went from personal career planning to mass anxiety. To users talking about how hard it is to stay motivated when they might lose their job very soon, maybe tomorrow." Meta has seen firsthand how morale can roil the workplace. In an internal email, chief technology officer Andrew Bosworth said the company's communication surrounding the restructuring of its AI division was "atrocious," Wired reported last week. The memo came on the tail of members of the 6,500-person Applied AI team expressing frustration toward their work to improve the company's AI models, which they said was made up of menial tasks with minimal interaction with other employees. Meta declined comment. "We've undermined the trust you have that your specific expertise and contribution will be valued, that you will grow and advance your career, and that this will be a place where you can actually have an impact," Bosworth wrote. "We shook up the management structure that was providing you stability while rapid changes in strategy, including the boom/bust cycle of hiring, left entire teams in the lurch." Bosworth said the company will take steps to be "fun and enjoyable" for employees, such as increasing travel budgets and social event spending, as well as "improving microkitchens" where workers can take breaks and eat snacks. "I hope we can rekindle the best of the culture we joined," Bosworth wrote. Jeffrey Pfeffer, a professor of organizational behavior at the Stanford Graduate School of Business, said employee unrest in the tech industry more broadly is a result of the "move fast and break things" tradition that often leaves workers vulnerable. "The tech industry has said people are the most important asset, but they never act that way," Pfeffer told Fortune . "Many people, I think, still go into jobs believing that their employers care about them and will take care of them, and so they are of course disappointed when they find that their employers actually don't care about them or will take care of them." The introduction of AI may complicate morale concerns, particularly because some of AI's greatest stalwarts—the engineers designing and training it—may be experiencing misgivings about the technology's advancements. While these workers are designing and optimizing the AI tools of tomorrow, there is also concern these tools will also replace them. A Gallup report published this month found that among U.S. tech workers who use AI at least monthly, the likelihood of being laid off is about 6%, a rate that triples to 18% among workers who use the technology less frequently. "We know that as tools come in, it often restructures jobs: Certain tasks disappear, other tasks appear. That is a stressful time, right?" Neil Thompson, an assistant professor of innovation and strategy at the MIT Sloan School of Management, told Fortune . "People don't know what those new tasks are going to look like. They can see old tasks being threatened, and that can also make it more intimidating, particularly when you have quite impressive results coming out." Anthropic has explored this tension in its own employees. A report from the company published earlier this month looked at recursive self-improvement, or AI's ability to better itself with its own capabilities. One worker expressed concern with the limitation of their own role in developing this technology. "On days where everything works well, I can't help but think nothing I do matters, everything is automated and better and faster than I ever will be," the employee said. "But then there are days where everything breaks and I don't understand why and I realize I have no idea what I've been up to anymore." The report also published comments from employees who said Claude has augmented their work and left humans in the driver's seat of selecting the direction for models to move. Anthropic touted Claude's ability to ship more than 800 application programming interface (API) error fixes in April, a task the company said would have taken a human four years to complete. There are ways to ease the feeling of threat some workers have in navigating AI advancements, Thompson said. Companies can prepare workers through reskilling, but also by being transparent in changes that may happen to labor as a result of automation, both for better and for worse. Historically, Thompson said, this has looked like fewer experts in certain positions, with wages rising for these workers, and in other areas, the number of roles expanding, with wages decreasing. "That's a tough thing, but often there are more opportunities for people to enter that field, because now more people are capable of doing that," Thompson said. "If we think about the morale of people in these areas, I think one thing that can help is to say, like, this is not all doom and gloom." This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

sources.title: Anthropic says its workforce has become less junior and is spending more time in meetings
passages: Anthropic also says that technical teams now represent a smaller share of the overall workforce, falling from 61% to 56% — a trend that it attributes to “natural expansion of business functions as the company scales,” as well as “coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves.”

One employee reportedly described an “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything.” In an April 2026 survey, 27% of employees said they had become more productive because of Claude and 20% said their job had shifted “from actually doing work to managing Claudes”; apparently one engineered compared this to babysitting: “When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.”

Notably, Anthropic is making fewer junior hires, with the proportion of junior-level employees in technical departments falling from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and the proportion of junior technical hires falling even more sharply, from 27% to 9%.
The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year, according to a report that the AI company published on Friday.
The report says that based on calendar data, meeting time per employee is up 20% compared to a year ago, and it’s up 16% for technical contributors.

Anthropic argues that its own workplace trends could be indicators of “how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy,” especially since the company “has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI.” But even if other organizations never embrace AI as thoroughly or in the exact same way as Anthropic, the report offers an intriguing glimpse at how the company currently operates.

sources.title: Anthropic's AI Workforce Experiment is Already Squeezing Out Junior Jobs as Agents Work Six Times More Than Staff - International Business Times, Singapore Edition
passages: Anthropic's AI agents are now working six times as many hours as the employees directing them, while the share of junior workers among new technical hires has plunged from 27% to 9% — offering an early glimpse of how AI could reshape white-collar hiring, productivity and the structure of work.
Anthropic's agent data shows how deeply AI has penetrated its operations.
In March 2026, autonomous and interactive agent work hours surpassed human work hours for the first time.
The findings come from Anthropic 's new report, which draws on internal employment, AI-use, output, survey, communication, calendar and hiring data, alongside interviews with 17 employees.
A study following 192 engineers who adopted coding agents and 74 who did not found that the amount of code added rose sharply after adoption.
Anthropic cautioned that more code does not automatically mean better code or greater business impact, but said it found no difference in certain measures of code subsequently removed or reverted.
The company found that even non-technical employees generate enough AI output to require more than half a working week to read everything.
As a result, workers are increasingly doing what Anthropic calls "meta-work", building tools to monitor agents, writing instructions, creating dashboards and reviewing one agent's work with another.
The second Anthropic study shows why its employees may see this transformation differently from the wider public.
On average, Anthropic staff expect AI to perform 75% of their current work by 2030, compared with 28% among U.S. workers.
At the same time, technical departments accounted for 56% of Anthropic's workforce, down from 61% a year earlier.
Technical hiring continued to rise in absolute numbers, but sales, finance and recruiting grew faster.
The biggest employment shift is happening at the entry level.
Job postings for junior roles also declined sharply from December 2025.
Yet Anthropic employees do not expect automation to mean the company stops hiring.
Ninety-five percent expect Anthropic's headcount to grow over the next 12 months, with the median employee expecting 66% growth.
Anthropic stresses these are employees' personal expectations, not company plans.

Anthropic said interactive Claude sessions spend around 80% of their time waiting for human input, meaning the agents themselves are often ready to continue while employees become the limiting factor.

Anthropic said engineers' code commits rose to five times their velocity six months earlier, while lawyers processed more contracts, accounts-payable workers handled more invoices and salespeople closed more deals.

Weâ€™re publishing this research because Anthropic runs roughly a year and a half ahead of the economy on AI adoption, so what happens at Anthropic could be a leading indicator for the broader world.And we hope that it gives policymakers, researchers, and workers lead time to prepare for the economic impacts of the future â€“ and take steps now to make sure everyone benefits from AI.
The shift began as teams increasingly found that Claude could handle work previously assigned to junior technical staff, including writing code and finding bugs.
"The thing that raised eyebrows was the uplift for performance engineers in particular and it basically overnight changed what we were looking for," Anthropic quoted one employee as saying.

It is that the composition of work may change before total employment does, with fewer entry-level technical jobs, broader responsibilities for remaining employees and a growing premium on people who can direct, evaluate and govern fleets of AI agents.
As Anthropic's researchers put it, "Employees increasingly see their work as managing teams of Claudes," while human attention and judgment remain the bottlenecks the system struggles to overcome.
The AI-driven productivity surge has created an unexpected constraint -- humans cannot keep up with the work their agents generate.
The change is also reshaping what Anthropic wants from new hires.
Hiring managers increasingly emphasize autonomy and judgment rather than narrow technical expertise and implementation skills.

Anthropic began implementing hackathons "just to make sure we're interacting together as a team," as well as pair programming lunches for employees to share how they're using Claude Code, Fung said.

Anthropic touted Claude's ability to ship more than 800 application programming interface (API) error fixes in April, a task the company said would have taken a human four years to complete.

"Where pairing was once about working through a tough problem together, it's now increasingly about seeing how a colleague uses these new tools and systems differently than you might, so even as more of the work shifts toward collaborating with agents, engineers keep learning from one another.

extraction.body: As the tech industry continues to scale AI use, some companies are hitting snags not in the technology itself, but in the human workforce developing and working alongside AI agents. Fiona Fung, the engineering leader of Anthropic's Claude Code and Cowork teams, said in a recent episode of Lenny's Podcast that agentic AI use in the workplace has increased so much it was making employees' work more solitary, pushing the company to intervene with other team-building activities. "The other thing that we found interesting on the Claude Code team is, after a while, we felt it could start being a lonely experience because we all started just working with our agents so much," she said. Anthropic began implementing hackathons "just to make sure we're interacting together as a team," as well as pair programming lunches for employees to share how they're using Claude Code, Fung said. She deemed both interventions successful. "When we do pairwise programming, we actually learn so much from each other," she said. "Every time I watch someone work, I learn something myself as well." An Anthropic spokesperson said the company is paying close attention to how its AI tools impact how employees work together. While Anthropic leaders like Fung said the company has adapted to challenges tech employees have faced as they increase AI use, the loneliness some tech employees are facing may shed light on a larger morale issue in a rapidly changing industry. There have been about 120,000 tech layoffs in 2026 so far, nearly equaling 2025's total. Some of the companies driving the layoffs, including Meta , which let go of 8,000 workers this year, have cited AI as the reason behind the reductions. Many tech employees left unscathed by layoffs are still reeling from changes to their work, as well as the anxiety these reductions and AI advancements bring. On the social media site Blind, a platform where verified anonymous users can discuss their workplaces, tech workers lamented low morale following layoff announcements and geopolitical uncertainty, as well as a changing culture of employees becoming less critical of leadership, which they link to risks of less innovation. "The whole mood has changed," Sunguk Moon, cofounder and CEO of Blind, told the New York Times last month. "It went from personal career planning to mass anxiety. To users talking about how hard it is to stay motivated when they might lose their job very soon, maybe tomorrow." Meta has seen firsthand how morale can roil the workplace. In an internal email, chief technology officer Andrew Bosworth said the company's communication surrounding the restructuring of its AI division was "atrocious," Wired reported last week. The memo came on the tail of members of the 6,500-person Applied AI team expressing frustration toward their work to improve the company's AI models, which they said was made up of menial tasks with minimal interaction with other employees. Meta declined comment. "We've undermined the trust you have that your specific expertise and contribution will be valued, that you will grow and advance your career, and that this will be a place where you can actually have an impact," Bosworth wrote. "We shook up the management structure that was providing you stability while rapid changes in strategy, including the boom/bust cycle of hiring, left entire teams in the lurch." Bosworth said the company will take steps to be "fun and enjoyable" for employees, such as increasing travel budgets and social event spending, as well as "improving microkitchens" where workers can take breaks and eat snacks. "I hope we can rekindle the best of the culture we joined," Bosworth wrote. Jeffrey Pfeffer, a professor of organizational behavior at the Stanford Graduate School of Business, said employee unrest in the tech industry more broadly is a result of the "move fast and break things" tradition that often leaves workers vulnerable. "The tech industry has said people are the most important asset, but they never act that way," Pfeffer told Fortune . "Many people, I think, still go into jobs believing that their employers care about them and will take care of them, and so they are of course disappointed when they find that their employers actually don't care about them or will take care of them." The introduction of AI may complicate morale concerns, particularly because some of AI's greatest stalwarts—the engineers designing and training it—may be experiencing misgivings about the technology's advancements. While these workers are designing and optimizing the AI tools of tomorrow, there is also concern these tools will also replace them. A Gallup report published this month found that among U.S. tech workers who use AI at least monthly, the likelihood of being laid off is about 6%, a rate that triples to 18% among workers who use the technology less frequently. "We know that as tools come in, it often restructures jobs: Certain tasks disappear, other tasks appear. That is a stressful time, right?" Neil Thompson, an assistant professor of innovation and strategy at the MIT Sloan School of Management, told Fortune . "People don't know what those new tasks are going to look like. They can see old tasks being threatened, and that can also make it more intimidating, particularly when you have quite impressive results coming out." Anthropic has explored this tension in its own employees. A report from the company published earlier this month looked at recursive self-improvement, or AI's ability to better itself with its own capabilities. One worker expressed concern with the limitation of their own role in developing this technology. "On days where everything works well, I can't help but think nothing I do matters, everything is automated and better and faster than I ever will be," the employee said. "But then there are days where everything breaks and I don't understand why and I realize I have no idea what I've been up to anymore." The report also published comments from employees who said Claude has augmented their work and left humans in the driver's seat of selecting the direction for models to move. Anthropic touted Claude's ability to ship more than 800 application programming interface (API) error fixes in April, a task the company said would have taken a human four years to complete. There are ways to ease the feeling of threat some workers have in navigating AI advancements, Thompson said. Companies can prepare workers through reskilling, but also by being transparent in changes that may happen to labor as a result of automation, both for better and for worse. Historically, Thompson said, this has looked like fewer experts in certain positions, with wages rising for these workers, and in other areas, the number of roles expanding, with wages decreasing. "That's a tough thing, but often there are more opportunities for people to enter that field, because now more people are capable of doing that," Thompson said. "If we think about the morale of people in these areas, I think one thing that can help is to say, like, this is not all doom and gloom." This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

sources.title: Anthropic says its workforce has become less junior and is spending more time in meetings
passages: Anthropic also says that technical teams now represent a smaller share of the overall workforce, falling from 61% to 56% — a trend that it attributes to “natural expansion of business functions as the company scales,” as well as “coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves.”

One employee reportedly described an “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything.” In an April 2026 survey, 27% of employees said they had become more productive because of Claude and 20% said their job had shifted “from actually doing work to managing Claudes”; apparently one engineered compared this to babysitting: “When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.”

Notably, Anthropic is making fewer junior hires, with the proportion of junior-level employees in technical departments falling from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and the proportion of junior technical hires falling even more sharply, from 27% to 9%.
The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year, according to a report that the AI company published on Friday.
The report says that based on calendar data, meeting time per employee is up 20% compared to a year ago, and it’s up 16% for technical contributors.

Anthropic argues that its own workplace trends could be indicators of “how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy,” especially since the company “has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI.” But even if other organizations never embrace AI as thoroughly or in the exact same way as Anthropic, the report offers an intriguing glimpse at how the company currently operates.

sources.title: Anthropic's AI Workforce Experiment is Already Squeezing Out Junior Jobs as Agents Work Six Times More Than Staff - International Business Times, Singapore Edition
passages: Anthropic's AI agents are now working six times as many hours as the employees directing them, while the share of junior workers among new technical hires has plunged from 27% to 9% — offering an early glimpse of how AI could reshape white-collar hiring, productivity and the structure of work.
Anthropic's agent data shows how deeply AI has penetrated its operations.
In March 2026, autonomous and interactive agent work hours surpassed human work hours for the first time.
The findings come from Anthropic 's new report, which draws on internal employment, AI-use, output, survey, communication, calendar and hiring data, alongside interviews with 17 employees.
A study following 192 engineers who adopted coding agents and 74 who did not found that the amount of code added rose sharply after adoption.
Anthropic cautioned that more code does not automatically mean better code or greater business impact, but said it found no difference in certain measures of code subsequently removed or reverted.
The company found that even non-technical employees generate enough AI output to require more than half a working week to read everything.
As a result, workers are increasingly doing what Anthropic calls "meta-work", building tools to monitor agents, writing instructions, creating dashboards and reviewing one agent's work with another.
The second Anthropic study shows why its employees may see this transformation differently from the wider public.
On average, Anthropic staff expect AI to perform 75% of their current work by 2030, compared with 28% among U.S. workers.
At the same time, technical departments accounted for 56% of Anthropic's workforce, down from 61% a year earlier.
Technical hiring continued to rise in absolute numbers, but sales, finance and recruiting grew faster.
The biggest employment shift is happening at the entry level.
Job postings for junior roles also declined sharply from December 2025.
Yet Anthropic employees do not expect automation to mean the company stops hiring.
Ninety-five percent expect Anthropic's headcount to grow over the next 12 months, with the median employee expecting 66% growth.
Anthropic stresses these are employees' personal expectations, not company plans.

Anthropic said interactive Claude sessions spend around 80% of their time waiting for human input, meaning the agents themselves are often ready to continue while employees become the limiting factor.

Anthropic said engineers' code commits rose to five times their velocity six months earlier, while lawyers processed more contracts, accounts-payable workers handled more invoices and salespeople closed more deals.

Weâ€™re publishing this research because Anthropic runs roughly a year and a half ahead of the economy on AI adoption, so what happens at Anthropic could be a leading indicator for the broader world.And we hope that it gives policymakers, researchers, and workers lead time to prepare for the economic impacts of the future â€“ and take steps now to make sure everyone benefits from AI.
The shift began as teams increasingly found that Claude could handle work previously assigned to junior technical staff, including writing code and finding bugs.
"The thing that raised eyebrows was the uplift for performance engineers in particular and it basically overnight changed what we were looking for," Anthropic quoted one employee as saying.

It is that the composition of work may change before total employment does, with fewer entry-level technical jobs, broader responsibilities for remaining employees and a growing premium on people who can direct, evaluate and govern fleets of AI agents.
As Anthropic's researchers put it, "Employees increasingly see their work as managing teams of Claudes," while human attention and judgment remain the bottlenecks the system struggles to overcome.
The AI-driven productivity surge has created an unexpected constraint -- humans cannot keep up with the work their agents generate.
The change is also reshaping what Anthropic wants from new hires.
Hiring managers increasingly emphasize autonomy and judgment rather than narrow technical expertise and implementation skills.

sources.title: Replit makes OpenAI its default over Anthropic, CEO says
passages: After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default.
This shift could significantly reduce Replit’s spend with Anthropic since most customers stick with the default rather than selecting a model themselves.
This article was originally published on October 16 at 2:22 pm PT.

“Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.”
That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s.
Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost.
Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer partnering with Anthropic.
One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place.

It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser.

extraction.body: Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt . Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer partnering with Anthropic. “I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.” It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser. After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default. This shift could significantly reduce Replit’s spend with Anthropic since most customers stick with the default rather than selecting a model themselves. Prior to striking a deal with OpenAI, Replit relied on Anthropic’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s. “Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.” Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place. There is evidence on the company’s website , blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was promoting Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities. Masad also shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue. “We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.” Backstage, Masad told TechCrunch that he expects more than half of Replit’s revenue to come from enterprise and government customers in 2027. Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures. “In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.” This article was originally published on October 16 at 2:22 pm PT. It has been updated to include more context around Replit’s partnerships with Anthropic and OpenAI. Its title has been updated, as well. extraction.body: Replit CEO Amjad Masad just dropped a bombshell at TechCrunch Disrupt: the coding platform hasn't been working with Anthropic for months. The revelation comes as a surprise to an industry that watched Replit announce an OpenAI partnership in August without any hint it was ditching Claude. Cost pressures drove the decision, Masad said, marking another win for OpenAI in the battle for developer platform partnerships. Replit just confirmed what it carefully avoided saying for months: it's done with Anthropic. CEO Amjad Masad made the disclosure at TechCrunch Disrupt, revealing the developer platform ended its partnership with the Claude maker for reasons that include cost. When Replit announced its OpenAI partnership back in August, the company framed it as an expansion, not a replacement. There was no mention of Anthropic getting the boot. Now, two months later, Masad is confirming what the silence already suggested: Replit picked a side, and OpenAI won. Cost emerged as a key factor in the decision, Masad said, though he pointed to "a number of different reasons" without elaborating further. For developer platforms like Replit that integrate AI models to power coding assistants and automation features, API costs can make or break unit economics. OpenAI has been aggressively pricing its models to win enterprise and platform deals, and that strategy appears to be paying off. The split adds to a rough stretch for Anthropic. Just days ago, the company found itself appealing a Pentagon AI blacklist in federal court, fighting to regain access to defense contracts. The Claude maker also recently opened its books to select investors amid growing IPO speculation, and granted unprecedented access to independent AI auditors in a transparency push. But transparency around partnerships hasn't been Anthropic's problem. While the company battles regulatory headwinds and safety concerns, OpenAI has been quietly locking down the developer platform ecosystem. The Replit win follows a string of high-profile integrations that have made GPT-4 and its successors the default choice for coding tools. The company recently saw VP of Infrastructure Sachin Katti exit to build a new venture, though he's staying on as an advisor. And an FBI arrest of a Saudi employee over a recording device raised fresh security questions. Still, none of that has slowed its momentum in signing platform deals. The San Francisco-based company has been scaling its AI-powered coding environment rapidly, and betting on the model provider with the deepest pockets and most aggressive pricing gives it room to grow without blowing up its cost structure. OpenAI's infrastructure investments and model performance improvements have made it the safe choice for platforms that need reliability at scale. What's striking is how Replit managed the transition. By announcing the OpenAI deal without mentioning Anthropic's exit, the company avoided the narrative of a breakup. Instead, it controlled the message: OpenAI was the new partner, and Anthropic simply faded into the background. Only now, with Masad's Disrupt comments, is the full picture emerging. The developer tools market has become a critical battleground for AI model providers. Platforms like Replit, GitHub Copilot, and Cursor represent millions of developers who will build muscle memory around whichever model powers their daily workflow. Losing Replit means Anthropic loses mindshare with a generation of coders who might have defaulted to Claude. Masad's disclosure also raises questions about what other partnerships might be quietly shifting. If cost is driving Replit away from Anthropic, other platforms facing similar economics could be reconsidering their model provider mix. OpenAI's scale advantages and willingness to undercut on price create a gravitational pull that's hard for competitors to counter. The Replit-Anthropic split isn't just about one partnership ending. It's a signal that cost and scale are starting to matter more than model differentiation in the platform wars. As OpenAI leverages its funding and infrastructure to offer aggressive pricing, competitors like Anthropic face a tough choice: match on price and sacrifice margins, or lose platform deals that shape developer defaults. For now, OpenAI is winning that battle, and Replit's quiet defection proves it.

extraction.body: Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt . Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer partnering with Anthropic. “I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.” It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser. After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default. This shift could significantly reduce Replit’s spend with Anthropic since most customers stick with the default rather than selecting a model themselves. Prior to striking a deal with OpenAI, Replit relied on Anthropic’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s. “Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.” Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place. There is evidence on the company’s website , blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was promoting Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities. Masad also shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue. “We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.” Backstage, Masad told TechCrunch that he expects more than half of Replit’s revenue to come from enterprise and government customers in 2027. Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures. “In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.” This article was originally published on October 16 at 2:22 pm PT. The revelation comes as a surprise to an industry that watched Replit announce an OpenAI partnership in August without any hint it was ditching Claude. Cost pressures drove the decision, Masad said, marking another win for OpenAI in the battle for developer platform partnerships. Replit just confirmed what it carefully avoided saying for months: it's done with Anthropic. CEO Amjad Masad made the disclosure at TechCrunch Disrupt, revealing the developer platform ended its partnership with the Claude maker for reasons that include cost. When Replit announced its OpenAI partnership back in August, the company framed it as an expansion, not a replacement. There was no mention of Anthropic getting the boot. Now, two months later, Masad is confirming what the silence already suggested: Replit picked a side, and OpenAI won. Cost emerged as a key factor in the decision, Masad said, though he pointed to "a number of different reasons" without elaborating further. For developer platforms like Replit that integrate AI models to power coding assistants and automation features, API costs can make or break unit economics. OpenAI has been aggressively pricing its models to win enterprise and platform deals, and that strategy appears to be paying off. The split adds to a rough stretch for Anthropic. Just days ago, the company found itself appealing a Pentagon AI blacklist in federal court, fighting to regain access to defense contracts. The Claude maker also recently opened its books to select investors amid growing IPO speculation, and granted unprecedented access to independent AI auditors in a transparency push. But transparency around partnerships hasn't been Anthropic's problem. While the company battles regulatory headwinds and safety concerns, OpenAI has been quietly locking down the developer platform ecosystem. The Replit win follows a string of high-profile integrations that have made GPT-4 and its successors the default choice for coding tools. The company recently saw VP of Infrastructure Sachin Katti exit to build a new venture, though he's staying on as an advisor. And an FBI arrest of a Saudi employee over a recording device raised fresh security questions. Still, none of that has slowed its momentum in signing platform deals. The San Francisco-based company has been scaling its AI-powered coding environment rapidly, and betting on the model provider with the deepest pockets and most aggressive pricing gives it room to grow without blowing up its cost structure. OpenAI's infrastructure investments and model performance improvements have made it the safe choice for platforms that need reliability at scale. What's striking is how Replit managed the transition. By announcing the OpenAI deal without mentioning Anthropic's exit, the company avoided the narrative of a breakup. Instead, it controlled the message: OpenAI was the new partner, and Anthropic simply faded into the background. Only now, with Masad's Disrupt comments, is the full picture emerging. The developer tools market has become a critical battleground for AI model providers. The gains cannot simply be multiplied together.

The experiment tests part of that engineering approach, rather than providing another 40-fold reduction in the estimated cost of attacking bitcoin.

extraction.body: Google says its Willow quantum chip has cut errors about 40-fold when preparing special states used in quantum calculations, tackling a costly step toward building machines powerful enough to crack bitcoin wallets. The result, published in Science this week, deals with something that rarely comes up in the bitcoin quantum debate — which usually focuses on how big a machine an attacker would need while underplaying how much of that machine would be occupied getting ready to calculate. A bitcoin wallet uses a secret key to approve payments and a matching public key that lets the network check those approvals. Spending typically reveals the public key, while some payment types expose it from the start. Working backward from it to the secret is supposed to take an impractical amount of computing, which makes it practically impossible to reverse-engineer crypto wallets. However, a large enough quantum computer running Shor’s algorithm could, in theory, do that math. Whoever recovered the secret key could sign transactions as the owner, and the network would accept them as genuine. Mathematician Peter Shor first published the method in 1994, but nobody has yet managed to demonstrate it. A recovery phrase locked in a physical drawer offers no protection against that, as the attacker would be working from information already sitting on the blockchain. Some later payment formats hide the public key behind a hash, a digital fingerprint, until the owner spends. An attacker targeting a previously hidden key would have to wait for that exposure and might need to recover the secret quickly enough to interfere with the payment. That is also why lost coins present a difficult problem. Bitcoin can introduce stronger spending protections, but someone still needs the existing keys to move old holdings into them. If those keys are lost, the owner cannot make the move. The exposed public key remains available to a future attacker. Some of bitcoin’s oldest holdings have had their public keys exposed since they were mined. Old coins have also been moving as the quantum debate grows louder. On Oct. 7, 100.02 BTC untouched since July 2010 moved after more than 16 years , carrying a value of about $8.5 million. In August, six wallets inactive since 2011–2014 moved another 553.59 BTC , worth roughly $40 million at the time. Those transfers do not singularly establish that holders are responding to quantum fears, as moving coins can even mean changing wallets, reorganizing holdings or preparing to sell. Quantum computers store information in units called qubits, which are extremely fragile. Heat, vibration and stray signals can disturb them and introduce errors, and adding more qubits also adds more opportunities for mistakes. Engineers deal with that by organizing many physical qubits into groups that detect and correct errors. Each group behaves like a more dependable unit, known as a logical qubit. Those units then need the digital equivalent of fuel to run certain operations, specially prepared quantum states that researchers call “magic states.” Each one is consumed when used, so the computer has to keep producing them throughout a calculation. Think of a restaurant kitchen where every dish needs a fresh batch of a sauce that cannot be reused, where some of the staff must keep making sauce while the others cook. In a quantum computer, hardware devoted to producing magic states is hardware that cannot be assigned to other work. Google’s method, called cultivation, starts with a rough version of the state, checks it for errors and throws out flawed attempts. The goal is to produce clean states using less hardware than older methods needed. The firm reported about 99.99% fidelity, a measure of how closely the finished states matched what researchers were aiming for. That number applies only to the states that passed inspection. Willow kept about 8% of its attempts after the checks during preparation and measurement. For every 100 tries, about eight made it through. The next steps include running the process at a much larger scale and keeping those states useful as they feed into longer calculations. The researchers say more work is needed on real-time operations and moving the states into stronger error-correcting setups. In March, Google estimated that a future superconducting quantum computer with fewer than 500,000 physical qubits could break the wallet cryptography used by Bitcoin and Ethereum, under a specific set of hardware assumptions. In September, CoinDesk reported on researchers cutting the workload of a core calculation used in that attack. That work covered one component, leaving out the complete attack and the physical hardware costs of running it. Those studies reduce the amount of math an attacker has to do. Cultivation addresses the cost of supplying the machine while it does that math. The gains cannot simply be multiplied together. Google’s March estimate already assumed efficient magic-state production. The experiment tests part of that engineering approach, rather than providing another 40-fold reduction in the estimated cost of attacking bitcoin. The March paper also shows how much fuel an attack would burn. For one modeled attack lasting about nine minutes after a public key becomes available, Google estimated the machine would need roughly 500,000 sufficiently reliable magic states every second. The firm reported about 99.99% fidelity, a measure of how closely the finished states matched what researchers were aiming for.

That number applies only to the states that passed inspection. Willow kept about 8% of its attempts after the checks during preparation and measurement. For every 100 tries, about eight made it through.

The next steps include running the process at a much larger scale and keeping those states useful as they feed into longer calculations. The researchers say more work is needed on real-time operations and moving the states into stronger error-correcting setups.

In March, Google estimated that a future superconducting quantum computer with fewer than 500,000 physical qubits could break the wallet cryptography used by Bitcoin and Ethereum, under a specific set of hardware assumptions.

In September, CoinDesk reported on researchers cutting the workload of a core calculation used in that attack. That work covered one component, leaving out the complete attack and the physical hardware costs of running it.
Those studies reduce the amount of math an attacker has to do. Cultivation addresses the cost of supplying the machine while it does that math.

The gains cannot simply be multiplied together. Google’s March estimate already assumed efficient magic-state production. The experiment tests part of that engineering approach, rather than providing another 40-fold reduction in the estimated cost of attacking bitcoin.

The March paper also shows how much fuel an attack would burn. For one modeled attack lasting about nine minutes after a public key becomes available, Google estimated the machine would need roughly 500,000 sufficiently reliable magic states every second.

Willow chip reduces errors in targeted quantum states by about 40-fold. Quantum breakthrough reopens debate over Bitcoin's long-term security, despite no immediate threat. Google’s Quantum AI team said its Willow processor cut errors in a critical class of quantum states by roughly 40-fold, achieving what researchers described as a record 99.99% logical fidelity. Google’s Willow chip can prepare the special quantum states needed for advanced calculations with about 40 times fewer errors, reducing one of the hardware bottlenecks behind any future attempt to crack bitcoin wallets. Google’s method, called magic state cultivation, starts with an imperfect state and runs it through a series of checks, discarding the attempts that fail. Google cautioned that the technique still needs to be validated at larger scales before it can support practical quantum computers, and it has not announced a timeline for scaling the method to systems large enough for cryptographic attacks. Google’s Willow experiment focused on producing high-quality “magic states” needed for complex operations, and the result did not mean anyone can drain Bitcoin wallets today. Google’s Willow chip contains only 105 physical qubits, a tiny fraction of what would be required to break the elliptic curve digital signature algorithm that secures Bitcoin transactions. Google’s latest magic state research does not demonstrate an ability to break Bitcoin’s cryptography, but it addresses one of the technical obstacles to developing machines that might eventually do so. Bull Theory said, “So Bitcoin is not in trouble today. extraction.body: Google says its Willow quantum chip has cut errors about 40-fold when preparing special states used in quantum calculations, tackling a costly step toward building machines powerful enough to crack bitcoin wallets. The result, published in Science this week, deals with something that rarely comes up in the bitcoin quantum debate — which usually focuses on how big a machine an attacker would need while underplaying how much of that machine would be occupied getting ready to calculate. A bitcoin wallet uses a secret key to approve payments and a matching public key that lets the network check those approvals. Spending typically reveals the public key, while some payment types expose it from the start. Working backward from it to the secret is supposed to take an impractical amount of computing, which makes it practically impossible to reverse-engineer crypto wallets. However, a large enough quantum computer running Shor’s algorithm could, in theory, do that math. Whoever recovered the secret key could sign transactions as the owner, and the network would accept them as genuine. Mathematician Peter Shor first published the method in 1994, but nobody has yet managed to demonstrate it. A recovery phrase locked in a physical drawer offers no protection against that, as the attacker would be working from information already sitting on the blockchain. Some later payment formats hide the public key behind a hash, a digital fingerprint, until the owner spends. An attacker targeting a previously hidden key would have to wait for that exposure and might need to recover the secret quickly enough to interfere with the payment. That is also why lost coins present a difficult problem. Bitcoin can introduce stronger spending protections, but someone still needs the existing keys to move old holdings into them. If those keys are lost, the owner cannot make the move. The exposed public key remains available to a future attacker. Some of bitcoin’s oldest holdings have had their public keys exposed since they were mined. Old coins have also been moving as the quantum debate grows louder. On Oct. 7, 100.02 BTC untouched since July 2010 moved after more than 16 years , carrying a value of about $8.5 million. In August, six wallets inactive since 2011–2014 moved another 553.59 BTC , worth roughly $40 million at the time. Those transfers do not singularly establish that holders are responding to quantum fears, as moving coins can even mean changing wallets, reorganizing holdings or preparing to sell. Quantum computers store information in units called qubits, which are extremely fragile. Heat, vibration and stray signals can disturb them and introduce errors, and adding more qubits also adds more opportunities for mistakes. Engineers deal with that by organizing many physical qubits into groups that detect and correct errors. Each group behaves like a more dependable unit, known as a logical qubit. Those units then need the digital equivalent of fuel to run certain operations, specially prepared quantum states that researchers call “magic states.” Each one is consumed when used, so the computer has to keep producing them throughout a calculation. Think of a restaurant kitchen where every dish needs a fresh batch of a sauce that cannot be reused, where some of the staff must keep making sauce while the others cook. In a quantum computer, hardware devoted to producing magic states is hardware that cannot be assigned to other work. Google’s method, called cultivation, starts with a rough version of the state, checks it for errors and throws out flawed attempts. The goal is to produce clean states using less hardware than older methods needed. The firm reported about 99.99% fidelity, a measure of how closely the finished states matched what researchers were aiming for. That number applies only to the states that passed inspection. Willow kept about 8% of its attempts after the checks during preparation and measurement. For every 100 tries, about eight made it through. The next steps include running the process at a much larger scale and keeping those states useful as they feed into longer calculations. The researchers say more work is needed on real-time operations and moving the states into stronger error-correcting setups. In March, Google estimated that a future superconducting quantum computer with fewer than 500,000 physical qubits could break the wallet cryptography used by Bitcoin and Ethereum, under a specific set of hardware assumptions. In September, CoinDesk reported on researchers cutting the workload of a core calculation used in that attack. That work covered one component, leaving out the complete attack and the physical hardware costs of running it. Those studies reduce the amount of math an attacker has to do. Cultivation addresses the cost of supplying the machine while it does that math. The gains cannot simply be multiplied together. Google’s March estimate already assumed efficient magic-state production. The experiment tests part of that engineering approach, rather than providing another 40-fold reduction in the estimated cost of attacking bitcoin. The March paper also shows how much fuel an attack would burn. For one modeled attack lasting about nine minutes after a public key becomes available, Google estimated the machine would need roughly 500,000 sufficiently reliable magic states every second. passages: Fortunately, newer Galaxy Tab models come with longer software support cycles.
Samsung began its seven-year software update policy with the Galaxy Tab S10 series that launched in 2024.
Surprisingly, even Samsung's budget Galaxy Tab A11 and A11+ devices, which released in 2025, are eligible for seven years of Android and security updates.
If you're buying from Samsung's current catalog of tablets, you don't have to worry about having software updates dropped anytime soon.
Not every tablet Samsung has sold in previous years enjoys that kind of longevity, though.
Samsung also sells rugged tablets under its Galaxy Tab Active lineup, which are marketed primarily towards business and enterprise customers.
These tablets are the last ones released before Samsung's more generous support policy.
