Back in the TouchWiz era, Samsung's reputation for timely software updates wasn't exactly the best. It's thus great to see how far the brand has come in delivering faster updates and providing longer software support for its devices. Samsung is now one of the few Android manufacturers that offers a generously long software support policy, with its recent Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra benefiting from seven years of OS and security updates. Not every tablet Samsung has sold in previous years enjoys that kind of longevity, though. 2026 marks the final release of major Android updates for the Galaxy Tab S9, S9+, S9 Ultra, S9 FE and S9 FE+. These tablets will receive the One UI 9 update , which is based on Android 17. The Galaxy Tab S9 series arrived in 2023 running One UI 5.1 (Android 13), with Samsung promising four generations of major OS updates and five years of security patches for these devices. They should continue to receive security updates until sometime in 2028. The Galaxy Tab S8, S8+ and S8 Ultra (released in February 2022) have already received their final major OS upgrade with One UI 8, which is based on Android 16. Security updates should continue until February 2027. Android 16 is also the last major update for the Galaxy Tab A9 and A9+, which were released in October 2023. Despite being a bit newer, the Galaxy Tab A9 series has already received its final major OS update, likely because it was a budget-oriented offering. It will still receive another year of security updates. Fortunately, newer Galaxy Tab models come with longer software support cycles. Samsung began its seven-year software update policy with the Galaxy Tab S10 series that launched in 2024. The newer Galaxy Tab S11 and S12 models offer the same commitment. Surprisingly, even Samsung's budget Galaxy Tab A11 and A11+ devices, which released in 2025, are eligible for seven years of Android and security updates. If you're buying from Samsung's current catalog of tablets, you don't have to worry about having software updates dropped anytime soon. Samsung also sells rugged tablets under its Galaxy Tab Active lineup, which are marketed primarily towards business and enterprise customers. These devices have different software update policies. The Galaxy Tab Active5 was launched in 2024 with a four-year commitment to Android OS updates and five years of security updates. Since it shipped with Android 14, it should be good for updates through Android 18, with security patches continuing until 2029. Be aware that not every device from Samsung receives OS updates at the same time. Rollout schedules vary depending on your tablet's model and region. So if you aren't seeing the One UI 9 update on your Galaxy Tab yet, it doesn't mean you've been left out. Check for Android or security updates on your Samsung tablet by navigating to Settings > Software update > Download and install . If there's a pending update available, tap Install now .

sources.title: Samsung Galaxy update support up to 7 years; how long will my device be supported?
passages: 11 local time, Samsung smartphones support operating system updates for up to 7 years for flagship models, 5 to 6 years for mid-range models and about 4 years at most for entry-level models.This year, Android 17 led software changes for smartphones, focusing on productivity-enhancing features.

Samsung Electronics provides a list of devices eligible for security updates, which can be used to check current support status.If the last update date in the Settings app has been stuck for months or years rather than days, there is a high chance support has already ended.
In practice, the Galaxy A34 and A54 5G receive Android updates until March 2027, but the Galaxy A73 is no longer eligible from April 2026.Some tablet models receive longer support.

Wearable devices are also still eligible for updates this year, but the original text did not specify individual model names separately.The article also presented it as key that users must check Samsung device support themselves.

It said that if such signs appear, it may be necessary to consider when to replace the smartphone with a new one.Ultimately, Samsung device users in 2026 should first distinguish and check whether their model receives only security updates or also Android operating system updates.
The Galaxy Tab Active5 Pro will continue to be supported through 2033.
Even if a user finds a cheap refurbished model online, the price advantage can shrink if the device loses access to updates within that year.
In particular, when deciding whether to keep using an existing device or buy a used one, users should weigh the remaining support period first rather than the handset price.

As operating system updates are missed cumulatively, compatibility with apps designed for the latest versions also gradually declines.Along with this, signs of device abnormalities were cited as factors to watch in connection with the end of updates.
Engadget also warned that losing security patches can expose smartphones to various new attacks.In the secondhand market, these support periods are also an important criterion for judgment.
Engadget pointed out that this tendency is stronger in Samsung’s entry-level A series.

extraction.body: [DigitalToday reporter Jinju Hong] Some older Samsung Electronics Galaxy devices will continue to receive Android operating system updates in 2026, but support periods differ widely by product line.According to IT outlet Engadget on Oct. 11 local time, Samsung smartphones support operating system updates for up to 7 years for flagship models, 5 to 6 years for mid-range models and about 4 years at most for entry-level models.This year, Android 17 led software changes for smartphones, focusing on productivity-enhancing features. Samsung Electronics has already applied One UI 9 based on Android 17 to the Galaxy Fold8 series and the Flip8. Unlike the latest devices, older models run security updates and operating system updates differently. Security patches are provided for a relatively long time, but operating system updates that include feature changes often end earlier.The gap in support periods is more pronounced in the Galaxy A series. Engadget pointed out that this tendency is stronger in Samsung’s entry-level A series. In practice, the Galaxy A34 and A54 5G receive Android updates until March 2027, but the Galaxy A73 is no longer eligible from April 2026.Some tablet models receive longer support. The Galaxy Tab Active5 supports Android updates until January 2028. The Galaxy Tab Active5 Pro will continue to be supported through 2033. Wearable devices are also still eligible for updates this year, but the original text did not specify individual model names separately.The article also presented it as key that users must check Samsung device support themselves. Manufacturers often do not warn in advance when software or security updates end. The article said manufacturers do not separately notify users before stopping updates, and advised users to look up their smartphone model online to confirm. extraction.body: These tablets are the last ones released before Samsung's more generous support policy. Back in the TouchWiz era, Samsung's reputation for timely software updates wasn't exactly the best. It's thus great to see how far the brand has come in delivering faster updates and providing longer software support for its devices. Samsung is now one of the few Android manufacturers that offers a generously long software support policy, with its recent Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra benefiting from seven years of OS and security updates. Not every tablet Samsung has sold in previous years enjoys that kind of longevity, though. 2026 marks the final release of major Android updates for the Galaxy Tab S9, S9+, S9 Ultra, S9 FE and S9 FE+. These tablets will receive the One UI 9 update , which is based on Android 17. The Galaxy Tab S9 series arrived in 2023 running One UI 5.1 (Android 13), with Samsung promising four generations of major OS updates and five years of security patches for these devices. They should continue to receive security updates until sometime in 2028. The Galaxy Tab S8, S8+ and S8 Ultra (released in February 2022) have already received their final major OS upgrade with One UI 8, which is based on Android 16. Security updates should continue until February 2027. Android 16 is also the last major update for the Galaxy Tab A9 and A9+, which were released in October 2023. Despite being a bit newer, the Galaxy Tab A9 series has already received its final major OS update, likely because it was a budget-oriented offering. It will still receive another year of security updates. Fortunately, newer Galaxy Tab models come with longer software support cycles. Samsung began its seven-year software update policy with the Galaxy Tab S10 series that launched in 2024. The newer Galaxy Tab S11 and S12 models offer the same commitment. Surprisingly, even Samsung's budget Galaxy Tab A11 and A11+ devices, which released in 2025, are eligible for seven years of Android and security updates. If you're buying from Samsung's current catalog of tablets, you don't have to worry about having software updates dropped anytime soon. Samsung also sells rugged tablets under its Galaxy Tab Active lineup, which are marketed primarily towards business and enterprise customers. These devices have different software update policies. The Galaxy Tab Active5 was launched in 2024 with a four-year commitment to Android OS updates and five years of security updates. Since it shipped with Android 14, it should be good for updates through Android 18, with security patches continuing until 2029. Be aware that not every device from Samsung receives OS updates at the same time. Rollout schedules vary depending on your tablet's model and region. So if you aren't seeing the One UI 9 update on your Galaxy Tab yet, it doesn't mean you've been left out. Check for Android or security updates on your Samsung tablet by navigating to Settings > Software update > Download and install . If there's a pending update available, tap Install now .

PDF apps are a dime a dozen, and unlike a decade ago, you can find a full-fledged PDF editor like PDFGear completely for free . However, I had a very specific requirement: I couldn't use an online PDF editor due to the sensitivity of the documents, but still needed it to be accessible for every employee in an organization, so desktop PDF apps weren't going to cut it. While looking for some open-source or self-hosted solutions, I found BentoPDF. A versatile PDF tool that I could self-host via Docker, and completely free to use. Your PDF fonts shouldn’t vanish when you edit. BentoPDF is an open-source PDF toolkit that you can either use through its hosted web version or self-host on your own server using Docker. Since my whole reason for looking at it was keeping sensitive documents off third-party servers, the self-hosted route was the obvious pick. All processing happens client-side in your browser, so even when you're running it on a server, the files never leave your machine. The feature list is broad enough that it replaced most of what I used Adobe Acrobat for. You get fillable form creation, which was the main draw for me, along with a redaction and annotation editor, PDF compression, format conversion to and from over a dozen file types, metadata stripping, and a multi-tool page manager that handles merging, splitting, rotating, and reordering. There are other free PDF tools that cover some of these tasks , but few bundle everything into a single self-hosted package with no upload limits and no subscription. For someone deciding whether BentoPDF is worth their time, the short answer is yes, if your workflow revolves around form filling, annotations, and document management rather than direct text editing. More on that limitation later. BentoPDF offers a few installation options, including a bare-metal install, but the recommended and fastest route is Docker Compose. To set up BentoPDF, you need Docker installed before anything else. If you don't have it, download Docker Desktop , run the installer, and wait until the system tray icon shows Docker Desktop is running . On Windows, Docker will ask you to enable WSL 2 during setup. Accept that, restart if prompted, and you're good. Once Docker is ready, open a terminal. On Windows, use PowerShell. On macOS or Linux, the default terminal works. BentoPDF ships in two image variants: the standard version includes BentoPDF's marketing pages alongside the tools, while the "Simple Mode" image strips those out and shows only the tools. For internal or company use, Simple Mode is the cleaner option. The install steps are the same for both; you just use a different image tag. Create a new folder anywhere on your drive, open it in your terminal, and create a file called docker-compose.yml with the following content: Then run Docker compose up -d in the same folder. The -d flag runs it in the background so you can close the terminal without stopping BentoPDF. It will now survive reboots and start itself back up whenever Docker launches. If you eventually want BentoPDF accessible over the internet with a custom domain like pdf.yourdomain.com, you would pair it with a reverse proxy such as Nginx Proxy Manager or Caddy, point a DNS record at your server's public IP, and request an SSL certificate so the connection is encrypted. That's a separate project and not strictly necessary for local or LAN use, but worth exploring once you're comfortable with the basics. Docker Desktop is a one-click application for Windows, macOS, and Linux for easily building, running, and managing containerized applications. The biggest limitation is direct text editing. Adobe Acrobat and even free desktop apps like PDFGear let you click into existing paragraphs and edit the text like a word processor. BentoPDF can't do that. Its own roadmap lists direct PDF content editing as a planned feature, but right now, you're limited to annotating, redacting, and adding new form fields or stamps on top of a document. If you need to rewrite body text, you'll still need a separate PDF editor. There's also no native desktop or mobile app. BentoPDF is entirely browser-based, whether you're using the hosted version or self-hosting it. That's part of its privacy appeal, but it means no offline experience and no app store install. And unlike Acrobat or PDFGear, there's no AI-powered summarization, which is consistent with its privacy-first stance, but worth noting if that's something you rely on. For my use case, though, none of these were deal-breakers. I didn't need a full-fledged editor. I needed a way to fill forms, annotate documents, and make all of that accessible to a team without uploading anything to a third-party service. And BentoPDF does exactly that. BentoPDF is a free, open-source, privacy-first PDF toolkit that runs entirely in your browser (or self-hosted), merging, splitting, compressing, converting, and editing PDFs with zero uploads or tracking. BentoPDF is a strong choice if you care more about privacy and control over where your PDFs are processed than having every feature under one roof. Yes, it doesn't have direct text editing, and a few other things like native apps, AI features, and enterprise-grade signing workflows might still be part of the roadmap and could take a while to land. But for form filling, annotations, compression, and format conversion on a server you own, it already does enough to replace a paid subscription. extraction.body: I know I am just a drop in the ocean of people who've grown tired of artificial intelligence worming its way into everything. AI can legitimately improve our lives in many ways, but it also often makes things more complicated than they need to be. This sentiment applies to everything from simple productivity apps to creative tools. Few places show this overreliance on AI more than modern smartphones. With every new update on my Android device, I feel like AI is being forced into my life where it doesn't belong. My response has been to find replacements for all these AI-bloated, pre-installed apps, creating a much quieter, less intrusive experience where at least some of my data isn't being siphoned off and sold to the highest bidder. I'm one of the people who has pretty staunchly stuck to Google Maps for an incredibly long time. It's not necessarily because I think it's the best, but it is reasonably reliable, unlike some other mainstream map apps. Like a lot of people, AI fatigue is hitting me pretty hard, and the more Google tries to force artificial intelligence on me in Maps, the more I feel the urge to rebel and go back to a simpler, less intrusive app instead. This is where Organic Maps comes in. While Google Maps comes out ahead in real-time traffic updates and a database of businesses tied to its map app, I've been happy to trade those features for a simpler setup. When you boot up Organic Maps, it will download data for your region, which is crowdsourced via OpenStreetMaps and maintained by global volunteers. After this, it offers fully offline functionality. There is no intrusive AI nonsense, and I feel like my data is more secure. It is incredibly privacy-focused, with zero ads, no account login needed, and no background tracking. I have tried a lot of different keyboards recently, looking for an alternative to Gboard or Samsung Keyboard. I think a keyboard is one of the last things that needs an internet connection or AI integration. In my anecdotal experience, AI integration in keyboards has made things like predictive text, input registration, and autocorrect worse. There is also, once again, the argument that uploading every keystroke to some cloud-based AI is dubious for privacy and security. I've jumped from keyboard to keyboard looking for a good alternative, trying things from TypeWise to FUTO keyboard . The least intrusive and most intuitive one I found, however, was Simple Keyboard, which makes a lot of sense given its name. It is lightweight, open-source, and refreshingly minimalist. It doesn't do much beyond acting like a keyboard, but that is exactly what makes it so appealing to me. Many people will feel differently, but the last place that I need an AI tool is my notes app. I understand the benefits, but all that I want to do in my notes app is to scribble things down every now and then, like grocery lists or other random things I don't want to forget. I don't need an AI tool analyzing my notes and drawing conclusions, because those conclusions are meaningless to me. Unfortunately, many mainstream apps in this category try to force AI features on you. The alternative that I found to replace these AI-integrated notes apps is Obsidian. What I love about Obsidian is how much choice you have. It can be as simple or as complicated as you like. It also prioritizes privacy, storing all notes locally as plain text files. The core app is free and works offline, but you can pay for Obsidian Sync to access their cloud service. Obsidian is extremely versatile . It is a blank-slate app, which is great for my use case, but it also offers extensive customization and a ton of optional integrations in the form of shortcuts and plug-ins if you're willing to play around with it. Integrating artificial intelligence into mainstream gallery and camera apps is extremely frustrating and a little concerning to me. Obviously, the privacy risks are big, and uploading personal libraries to cloud-based AI tools is another weak link in an already questionable security chain. More importantly, I feel that AI has taken the fun and the art out of photo editing. Everything has become homogenized, and honestly, a little dull. Really, any app in the Fossify suite could apply to this list. It is a collection of open-source, ad-free, privacy-focused apps created by the community as a fork of Simple Mobile Tools. The Fossify Gallery app is one of my favorites, though. It saves all media locally and doesn't request any internet permissions. There are no ads or hidden fees either. Most importantly, there are no AI tools. I think photography and photo editing are fun, and fun, creative things should be left to people rather than machines. I won't put on my tinfoil hat and go full conspiracy theorist, but the more AI gets integrated into my personal devices and the more I'm forced to use it, the more claustrophobic I feel. Using some of these de-bloated tools that don't use AI has made my phone a lot less stressful, and it hasn't noticeably decreased my productivity. I won't stop using AI altogether, but I am starting to question when and where it feels useful and when it's simply a gimmick. The Vivaldi browser is a breath of fresh non-ai air. coreStoryFacts.text: The feature list is broad enough that it replaced most of what I used Adobe Acrobat for.

You get fillable form creation, which was the main draw for me, along with a redaction and annotation editor, PDF compression, format conversion to and from over a dozen file types, metadata stripping, and a multi-tool page manager that handles merging, splitting, rotating, and reordering.
There are other free PDF tools that cover some of these tasks , but few bundle everything into a single self-hosted package with no upload limits and no subscription.
While looking for some open-source or self-hosted solutions, I found BentoPDF.
A versatile PDF tool that I could self-host via Docker, and completely free to use.
Since my whole reason for looking at it was keeping sensitive documents off third-party servers, the self-hosted route was the obvious pick.
The biggest limitation is direct text editing.
Adobe Acrobat and even free desktop apps like PDFGear let you click into existing paragraphs and edit the text like a word processor.
Its own roadmap lists direct PDF content editing as a planned feature, but right now, you're limited to annotating, redacting, and adding new form fields or stamps on top of a document.
If you need to rewrite body text, you'll still need a separate PDF editor.
Tashreef's fascination with consumer technology began in the school library when he stumbled upon a tech magazine, CHIP, which ultimately inspired him to pursue a degree in Computer Science.
Since 2012, Tashreef has professionally authored over a thousand how-to articles, contributing to Windows Report and How-To Geek.
He currently focuses on Microsoft Windows content at MakeUseOf, which he has been using since 2007.
BentoPDF is entirely browser-based, whether you're using the hosted version or self-hosting it.

However, I had a very specific requirement: I couldn't use an online PDF editor due to the sensitivity of the documents, but still needed it to be accessible for every employee in an organization, so desktop PDF apps weren't going to cut it.

extraction.body: Tashreef's fascination with consumer technology began in the school library when he stumbled upon a tech magazine, CHIP, which ultimately inspired him to pursue a degree in Computer Science. Since 2012, Tashreef has professionally authored over a thousand how-to articles, contributing to Windows Report and How-To Geek. He currently focuses on Microsoft Windows content at MakeUseOf, which he has been using since 2007. With hands-on experience building websites and technology blogs, he brings practical developer insights to his technical writing. You can view his complete work portfolio at itashreef.com. You might also stumble upon his short how-to video explainers, simplifying complex topics. Beyond writing, Tashreef enjoys creating short explainer videos, gaming, and exploring animated shows. PDF apps are a dime a dozen, and unlike a decade ago, you can find a full-fledged PDF editor like PDFGear completely for free . However, I had a very specific requirement: I couldn't use an online PDF editor due to the sensitivity of the documents, but still needed it to be accessible for every employee in an organization, so desktop PDF apps weren't going to cut it. While looking for some open-source or self-hosted solutions, I found BentoPDF. A versatile PDF tool that I could self-host via Docker, and completely free to use. Your PDF fonts shouldn’t vanish when you edit. BentoPDF is an open-source PDF toolkit that you can either use through its hosted web version or self-host on your own server using Docker. Since my whole reason for looking at it was keeping sensitive documents off third-party servers, the self-hosted route was the obvious pick. All processing happens client-side in your browser, so even when you're running it on a server, the files never leave your machine. The feature list is broad enough that it replaced most of what I used Adobe Acrobat for. You get fillable form creation, which was the main draw for me, along with a redaction and annotation editor, PDF compression, format conversion to and from over a dozen file types, metadata stripping, and a multi-tool page manager that handles merging, splitting, rotating, and reordering. There are other free PDF tools that cover some of these tasks , but few bundle everything into a single self-hosted package with no upload limits and no subscription. For someone deciding whether BentoPDF is worth their time, the short answer is yes, if your workflow revolves around form filling, annotations, and document management rather than direct text editing. More on that limitation later. BentoPDF offers a few installation options, including a bare-metal install, but the recommended and fastest route is Docker Compose. To set up BentoPDF, you need Docker installed before anything else. If you don't have it, download Docker Desktop , run the installer, and wait until the system tray icon shows Docker Desktop is running . On Windows, Docker will ask you to enable WSL 2 during setup. Accept that, restart if prompted, and you're good. Once Docker is ready, open a terminal. On Windows, use PowerShell. On macOS or Linux, the default terminal works. BentoPDF ships in two image variants: the standard version includes BentoPDF's marketing pages alongside the tools, while the "Simple Mode" image strips those out and shows only the tools. For internal or company use, Simple Mode is the cleaner option. The install steps are the same for both; you just use a different image tag. The fastest way to get BentoPDF running is a single command: For a more reliable setup that restarts automatically if your machine reboots, use Docker Compose instead. Create a new folder anywhere on your drive, open it in your terminal, and create a file called docker-compose.yml with the following content: Then run Docker compose up -d in the same folder. The -d flag runs it in the background so you can close the terminal without stopping BentoPDF. It will now survive reboots and start itself back up whenever Docker launches. If you eventually want BentoPDF accessible over the internet with a custom domain like pdf.yourdomain.com, you would pair it with a reverse proxy such as Nginx Proxy Manager or Caddy, point a DNS record at your server's public IP, and request an SSL certificate so the connection is encrypted. That's a separate project and not strictly necessary for local or LAN use, but worth exploring once you're comfortable with the basics. Docker Desktop is a one-click application for Windows, macOS, and Linux for easily building, running, and managing containerized applications. The biggest limitation is direct text editing. Adobe Acrobat and even free desktop apps like PDFGear let you click into existing paragraphs and edit the text like a word processor. BentoPDF can't do that. Its own roadmap lists direct PDF content editing as a planned feature, but right now, you're limited to annotating, redacting, and adding new form fields or stamps on top of a document. If you need to rewrite body text, you'll still need a separate PDF editor. There's also no native desktop or mobile app. BentoPDF is entirely browser-based, whether you're using the hosted version or self-hosting it. That's part of its privacy appeal, but it means no offline experience and no app store install. And unlike Acrobat or PDFGear, there's no AI-powered summarization, which is consistent with its privacy-first stance, but worth noting if that's something you rely on. For my use case, though, none of these were deal-breakers. I didn't need a full-fledged editor. While looking for some open-source or self-hosted solutions, I found BentoPDF. A versatile PDF tool that I could self-host via Docker, and completely free to use.

BentoPDF is an open-source PDF toolkit that you can either use through its hosted web version or self-host on your own server using Docker. Since my whole reason for looking at it was keeping sensitive documents off third-party servers, the self-hosted route was the obvious pick. The feature list is broad enough that it replaced most of what I used Adobe Acrobat for. You get fillable form creation, which was the main draw for me, along with a redaction and annotation editor, PDF compression, format conversion to and from over a dozen file types, metadata stripping, and a multi-tool page manager that handles merging, splitting, rotating, and reordering. Then run Docker compose up -d in the same folder. The -d flag runs it in the background so you can close the terminal without stopping BentoPDF. It will now survive reboots and start itself back up whenever Docker launches.

If you eventually want BentoPDF accessible over the internet with a custom domain like pdf.yourdomain.com, you would pair it with a reverse proxy such as Nginx Proxy Manager or Caddy, point a DNS record at your server's public IP, and request an SSL certificate so the connection is encrypted. That's a separate project and not strictly necessary for local or LAN use, but worth exploring once you're comfortable with the basics.
Docker Desktop is a one-click application for Windows, macOS, and Linux for easily building, running, and managing containerized applications.

The biggest limitation is direct text editing. Adobe Acrobat and even free desktop apps like PDFGear let you click into existing paragraphs and edit the text like a word processor. Its own roadmap lists direct PDF content editing as a planned feature, but right now, you're limited to annotating, redacting, and adding new form fields or stamps on top of a document. If you need to rewrite body text, you'll still need a separate PDF editor.

That's part of its privacy appeal, but it means no offline experience and no app store install. Like a lot of people, AI fatigue is hitting me pretty hard, and the more Google tries to force artificial intelligence on me in Maps, the more I feel the urge to rebel and go back to a simpler, less intrusive app instead.
While Google Maps comes out ahead in real-time traffic updates and a database of businesses tied to its map app, I've been happy to trade those features for a simpler setup.

extraction.body: I know I am just a drop in the ocean of people who've grown tired of artificial intelligence worming its way into everything. AI can legitimately improve our lives in many ways, but it also often makes things more complicated than they need to be. This sentiment applies to everything from simple productivity apps to creative tools. Few places show this overreliance on AI more than modern smartphones. With every new update on my Android device, I feel like AI is being forced into my life where it doesn't belong. My response has been to find replacements for all these AI-bloated, pre-installed apps, creating a much quieter, less intrusive experience where at least some of my data isn't being siphoned off and sold to the highest bidder. I'm one of the people who has pretty staunchly stuck to Google Maps for an incredibly long time. It's not necessarily because I think it's the best, but it is reasonably reliable, unlike some other mainstream map apps. Like a lot of people, AI fatigue is hitting me pretty hard, and the more Google tries to force artificial intelligence on me in Maps, the more I feel the urge to rebel and go back to a simpler, less intrusive app instead. This is where Organic Maps comes in. While Google Maps comes out ahead in real-time traffic updates and a database of businesses tied to its map app, I've been happy to trade those features for a simpler setup. When you boot up Organic Maps, it will download data for your region, which is crowdsourced via OpenStreetMaps and maintained by global volunteers. After this, it offers fully offline functionality. There is no intrusive AI nonsense, and I feel like my data is more secure. It is incredibly privacy-focused, with zero ads, no account login needed, and no background tracking. I have tried a lot of different keyboards recently, looking for an alternative to Gboard or Samsung Keyboard. I think a keyboard is one of the last things that needs an internet connection or AI integration. In my anecdotal experience, AI integration in keyboards has made things like predictive text, input registration, and autocorrect worse. There is also, once again, the argument that uploading every keystroke to some cloud-based AI is dubious for privacy and security. I've jumped from keyboard to keyboard looking for a good alternative, trying things from TypeWise to FUTO keyboard . The least intrusive and most intuitive one I found, however, was Simple Keyboard, which makes a lot of sense given its name. It is lightweight, open-source, and refreshingly minimalist. It doesn't do much beyond acting like a keyboard, but that is exactly what makes it so appealing to me. Many people will feel differently, but the last place that I need an AI tool is my notes app. I understand the benefits, but all that I want to do in my notes app is to scribble things down every now and then, like grocery lists or other random things I don't want to forget. I don't need an AI tool analyzing my notes and drawing conclusions, because those conclusions are meaningless to me. Unfortunately, many mainstream apps in this category try to force AI features on you. The alternative that I found to replace these AI-integrated notes apps is Obsidian. What I love about Obsidian is how much choice you have. It can be as simple or as complicated as you like. It also prioritizes privacy, storing all notes locally as plain text files. The core app is free and works offline, but you can pay for Obsidian Sync to access their cloud service. Obsidian is extremely versatile . It is a blank-slate app, which is great for my use case, but it also offers extensive customization and a ton of optional integrations in the form of shortcuts and plug-ins if you're willing to play around with it. Integrating artificial intelligence into mainstream gallery and camera apps is extremely frustrating and a little concerning to me. Obviously, the privacy risks are big, and uploading personal libraries to cloud-based AI tools is another weak link in an already questionable security chain. More importantly, I feel that AI has taken the fun and the art out of photo editing. Everything has become homogenized, and honestly, a little dull. Really, any app in the Fossify suite could apply to this list. It is a collection of open-source, ad-free, privacy-focused apps created by the community as a fork of Simple Mobile Tools. The Fossify Gallery app is one of my favorites, though. It saves all media locally and doesn't request any internet permissions. There are no ads or hidden fees either. Most importantly, there are no AI tools. I think photography and photo editing are fun, and fun, creative things should be left to people rather than machines. I won't put on my tinfoil hat and go full conspiracy theorist, but the more AI gets integrated into my personal devices and the more I'm forced to use it, the more claustrophobic I feel. Using some of these de-bloated tools that don't use AI has made my phone a lot less stressful, and it hasn't noticeably decreased my productivity. I won't stop using AI altogether, but I am starting to question when and where it feels useful and when it's simply a gimmick. The Vivaldi browser is a breath of fresh non-ai air. The best of How-To Geek, directly in your inbox.

A more compelling argument lies in Monero's thinner market. Over the years, many exchanges have delisted privacy coins due to stricter compliance regulations, which limits where they can be traded. A thinner market means fewer participants, leading to larger price swings from smaller trading volumes. Thus, while Monero has demonstrated relative resilience, the same market conditions could amplify its decline if selling pressure arises.

Partly yes. Monero's stability stems from its unique position in a privacy-focused market with dedicated holders, while external news and supply factors play only a minor role. However, there's also fragility; the smaller drop mainly reflects the limited number of sellers willing to act in this niche market, and that can shift quickly.

If the market narrative changes, we may first notice a divergence between Monero and Zcash. If Monero's decline from its all-time high surpasses Bitcoin's 33.9% while Zcash continues to rise, it could weaken the case for Monero maintaining its lead over Bitcoin.

Over the last 24 hours, Monero has gained 2.3%. Although it fell 2.2% over the past week, it is up 8.4% over the last 30 days. Meanwhile, Zcash (CRYPTO:ZEC), another prominent privacy coin, can also mask the sender, receiver, and amount of any transaction. Zcash rose by 2.2% in 24 hours and is up 8.9% over the past month.

These gains in Monero and Zcash stand out against most of the other 25 largest cryptocurrencies, which have mostly remained stagnant or declined. So what is Monero doing right that Bitcoin seems to be missing, or is this comparison simply skewed?

When we measure how far a coin has fallen from its peak, we get a sense of its resilience. This distance doesn't necessarily reflect a coin's quality, adoption, or future potential; sometimes, a coin stays close to its high simply because that high was lower initially.

Many successful investors eventually reach the same moment. The saving is done, the portfolio is built, and the question quietly changes from how much can I grow this to how much can I take out? Get that second question wrong and decades of good investing can come apart in a handful of years.

Market size can also explain part of the difference. Monero's market cap is around $10.4 billion, while Bitcoin's market cap sits at about $1.67 trillion, making Bitcoin roughly 160 times larger. Therefore, more capital needs to exit Bitcoin to affect its price than Monero.
Despite this, Monero's holders have sustained a smaller decline—30.6% as opposed to Bitcoin's 33.9%. This gap may reflect the different investor profiles in each coin.

Bitcoin's investors include those investing through exchange-traded funds (ETFs), corporate treasuries, and leveraged traders, many of whom might sell off their holdings during market downturns. In contrast, Monero lacks a U.S. spot ETF and has far less institutional ownership; its users tend to be individuals seeking private transaction capabilities, which may explain their tendency to hold through market declines.
Interestingly, both Monero and Zcash recorded gains without major upgrades, announcements, or regulatory news to drive them. Instead, price action has been the clearest indicator of market sentiment.

In the last 24 hours, Monero rose by 2.3%, while Zcash gained 2.2%, with both coins up 8.4% and 8.9%, respectively, over the past 30 days. When two privacy coins rise similarly in a market where most large cryptocurrencies have stagnated, a broader trend toward privacy is likely at play. This has put Zcash in the spotlight as one of the best trades of 2026.

Monero has a unique supply model known as "tail emission," where it provides miners with a small, consistent block reward indefinitely, unlike Bitcoin, which halves its reward on a fixed schedule until new issuance eventually stops altogether.

Some investors view Monero's ongoing issuance as a drawback since it adds to the total supply year after year. Thus, this factor does not necessarily clarify why Monero has held up better than Bitcoin.

A more compelling argument lies in Monero's thinner market. Over the years, many exchanges have delisted privacy coins due to stricter compliance regulations, which limits where they can be traded. A thinner market means fewer participants, leading to larger price swings from smaller trading volumes. Thus, while Monero has demonstrated relative resilience, the same market conditions could amplify its decline if selling pressure arises.

Partly yes. Monero's stability stems from its unique position in a privacy-focused market with dedicated holders, while external news and supply factors play only a minor role. However, there's also fragility; the smaller drop mainly reflects the limited number of sellers willing to act in this niche market, and that can shift quickly.

If the market narrative changes, we may first notice a divergence between Monero and Zcash. If Monero's decline from its all-time high surpasses Bitcoin's 33.9% while Zcash continues to rise, it could weaken the case for Monero maintaining its lead over Bitcoin.

In contrast, Bitcoin would need to rise from about $1.64 trillion to $2.53 trillion to hit a record.
To hit its record, Hyperliquid needs only a 22.9% increase, while Monero needs 42.9% and Bitcoin needs 54.7%.
This puts Hyperliquid in the lead based on price distance alone.
Monero, known for its privacy features that obscure transaction details, needs to maintain its upward momentum.
Over the week leading up to October 17, it rose 8.1%, while Bitcoin fell 1.5% and Hyperliquid fell 5.2%.
A critical network upgrade review on October 20 could flip…
Monero, on the other hand, has no maximum supply because of its tail emission, which rewards miners indefinitely.
Bitcoin has around 20.1 million coins in circulation with a hard cap of 21 million, so its dilution effect is minimal.
Hyperliquid faces challenges from scheduled token unlocks, which release team and community tokens and could increase selling pressure.
Additionally, when trading activity slows, its buyback mechanism weakens, often during price declines.
Moreover, Deribit is introducing over 90 USDC-settled contracts, which could split institutional trading volume across exchanges.
However, supply dilution—when more coins enter circulation—makes it harder for older prices to repeat.
This means its fully diluted value could reach approximately $93.6 billion at its record price.
Hyperliquid operates as a crypto exchange, specializing in perpetual futures—contracts that don’t expire and track price movements.
The platform spends about 97% to 99% of its trading fees to buy back and burn HYPE tokens, so higher trading volumes generally create consistent buying pressure.
As of September 26, about 47.5 million HYPE tokens had been removed from circulation, costing roughly $1.32 billion.
On October 15, Ripple Prime launched swaps on Hyperliquid markets, and on October 16, Pump. fun introduced Hyperliquid-powered perpetual futures.

The sustainability of this interest will greatly affect Monero’s next price move.
Bitcoin’s climb relies on renewed interest from spot ETF buyers.
These funds buy and hold Bitcoin directly and trade like stocks.
Kraken's parent company just announced plans to build on the Hyperliquid blockchain, sending HYPE soaring toward the $100 milestone.

Index-driven selling could dampen market sentiment, although companies are removed from the index only after failing the screening process in two consecutive annual filings.
Many exchanges have delisted privacy coins because of stricter compliance measures, leaving the market thin.
This makes Monero’s price susceptible to large swings with small orders.
Furthermore, it currently lacks a US spot ETF.

The sustainability of this interest will greatly affect Monero’s next price move.
Bitcoin’s climb relies on renewed interest from spot ETF buyers.
These funds buy and hold Bitcoin directly and trade like stocks.
Kraken's parent company just announced plans to build on the Hyperliquid blockchain, sending HYPE soaring toward the $100 milestone.
But the actual connection between this deal and the token's price is thinner than traders…
Bitcoin also faces a potential hurdle from index provider MSCI, which will implement new rules in November.

These rules will affect companies holding large amounts of digital assets , and Strategy Inc. ( NASDAQ: MSTR | MSTR Price Prediction ), which reported holding 846,000 bitcoins as of the second quarter, was flagged as possibly ineligible.
Index-driven selling could dampen market sentiment, although companies are removed from the index only after failing the screening process in two consecutive annual filings.
Many exchanges have delisted privacy coins because of stricter compliance measures, leaving the market thin.
This makes Monero’s price susceptible to large swings with small orders.
Furthermore, it currently lacks a US spot ETF.

extraction.body: NEW YORK, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Apple on Tuesday launched a raft of smart products, including an iPad-like device dubbed the HomeView, in a bet that its AI-upgraded Siri virtual assistant can help it carve out a bigger share of the highly competitive connected home market. The HomeView device, which starts at $299 and starts shipping next month, is Apple's latest entry into a highly competitive market for connected home devices. It will feature a 7-inch screen and face recognition and will help users control doorbells, thermostats and smart locks in a market where Apple has tinkered for a decade without major success. Apple is launching these products as it tries to fend off competition from rivals, including traditional competitors like Amazon.com, which has invested heavily in its Echo speakers and Ring doorbells and last week launched premium tablets, as well as newer AI upstarts like OpenAI that have hardware ambitions of their own. "Apple needs to demonstrate that its AI capabilities can deliver meaningful benefits beyond basic voice commands, simplifying everyday tasks and bringing greater intelligence to the home," said PP Foresight analyst Paolo Pescatore. Investors are looking more closely at Apple's hardware sales for growth. The company's services revenue has come under regulatory pressure, although that could also eventually get a boost from the new suite of devices. "The objective seems to be to drive high-margin 'Services' revenue via Apple TV, Apple Pay and iCloud," said Melissa Otto, head of Visible Alpha Research at S&P Global Market Intelligence, noting that Apple's 2027 services revenue is forecast to rise 12% to $138 billion. "Growth in Apple's lucrative subscription services may be the gateway to earnings growth increases over the next two years." Apple this summer upgraded Siri's capabilities with assistance from Google but analysts said it is unclear whether its AI assistant is competitive enough to lure consumers to a crowded connected home device space. The device features a 7-inch screen — which Apple said is to make it fit into a home without being too imposing — similar to Apple's "sunflower" iMac from the 2000s. And while it features a menu of square app icons like an iPhone or iPad that change depending on which user is recognized, Apple showed it being used more often via voice with its Siri AI assistant. The launches also coincide with growing worries that connected devices, including refrigerators and smart TVs, could be vulnerable to hackers. Apple accompanied the HomeView launch with updates to its HomePod smart speaker and Apple TV devices. It also introduced a range of accessories, including doorbells, cameras and thermostats, made by LG and Schneider Electric and designed with help from Apple. Apple's work with LG and Schneider Electric to sell a suite of products alongside the HomeView was meant to make it easier to add smart home products to a household. Kaiann Drance, Apple's vice president of product marketing for home products, said the devices can be added with a single tap, similar to Apple's first-party devices such as AirPods. "For people who haven't experienced the Home ecosystem or haven't gone further than maybe a product here or there, I think this is a great opportunity to look," Drance told Reuters in an interview. Ben Wood, chief analyst and chief marketing officer for CCS Insight, said that at first glance Apple's partnership with the two outside firms looked like a break with its usual practice of fully controlling its hardware. "However, looking closely, it appears like there has been very deep collaboration between Apple and these partners to ensure the design, engineering and experience closely match what users would expect from Apple," he said. During a video demonstrating the device, Apple showed the HomeView, which is meant to hang on walls or perch on tabletops, and its Siri virtual assistant juggling voice requests from multiple members of a family at the same time. To pull in private data from messages and calendars, the HomeView relies on a user having an iPhone that's been recently unlocked and connected to the same home network. The HomeView device will not be sold in the European Union, because Siri AI remains unavailable there due to EU regulations, Apple said. Apple first released its Home app to control smart gadgets in 2016, with HomePod smart speakers following in 2018, but those offerings are competing with Alphabet's Google Home speakers and Amazon's Echo line. Analysts said two major hurdles for Apple were making its devices work with a variety of third-party gadgets and the limited ability of Siri to give useful answers. “Apple has the brand, technology and loyal customers to make a serious impact, but it is playing catch-up with rivals that have a far stronger presence," Pescatore said. Fragmentation among various companies' "smart" home products and the difficulty of connecting them has proved a hurdle to the market's growth although there is hope that AI-enabled devices from Apple, Google and Amazon could make integration more seamless. "Most smart speakers and hubs in homes today are low-cost devices that can't run AI at the edge, so they are ripe for replacement," said Mohit Agrawal, Research Director at Counterpoint. "Amazon and Google have only just begun refreshing their hardware for Alexa+ and Gemini, so the upgrade cycle is wide open, and Apple wants to win it." Apple's $299 price for HomeView is above Amazon's Echo Show 8 at $199.99 and Google's Nest Hub at $99.99, as it seeks a bigger role in connected homes. The new Apple TV 4K enters the market at $299, more than double the price of its starting price of its predecessor and in line with Nvidia's Shield TV Pro, while rival offerings from Amazon, Google and Roku cost $200 or less. Shares were up about 1% in Tuesday afternoon trading after earlier touching a record. Apple stock has gained 25% so far this year, outperforming the large-cap Nasdaq 100, which is up 21% for the same period. (Reporting by Stephen Nellis in San Francisco; Additional reporting by Anhata Rooprai in Bengaluru; Editing by David Gaffen, Christian Plumb and Aurora Ellis)

Kaiann Drance, Apple's vice president of product marketing for home products, said the devices can be added with a single tap, similar to Apple's first-party devices such as AirPods.
"For people who haven't experienced the Home ecosystem or haven't gone further than maybe a product here or there, I think this is a great opportunity to look," Drance told Reuters in an interview.

Ben Wood, chief analyst and chief marketing officer for CCS Insight, said that at first glance Apple's partnership with the two outside firms looked like a break with its usual practice of fully controlling its hardware.

"However, looking closely, it appears like there has been very deep collaboration between Apple and these partners to ensure the design, engineering and experience closely match what users would expect from Apple," he said.

During a video demonstrating the device, Apple showed the HomeView, which is meant to hang on walls or perch on tabletops, and its Siri virtual assistant juggling voice requests from multiple members of a family at the same time.
To pull in private data from messages and calendars, the HomeView relies on a user having an iPhone that's been recently unlocked and connected to the same home network.
The HomeView device will not be sold in the European Union, because Siri AI remains unavailable there due to EU regulations, Apple said.

Apple first released its Home app to control smart gadgets in 2016, with HomePod smart speakers following in 2018, but those offerings are competing with Alphabet's Google Home speakers and Amazon's Echo line. Analysts said two major hurdles for Apple were making its devices work with a variety of third-party gadgets and the limited ability of Siri to give useful answers.
“Apple has the brand, technology and loyal customers to make a serious impact, but it is playing catch-up with rivals that have a far stronger presence," Pescatore said.

Fragmentation among various companies' "smart" home products and the difficulty of connecting them has proved a hurdle to the market's growth although there is hope that AI-enabled devices from Apple, Google and Amazon could make integration more seamless.

"Most smart speakers and hubs in homes today are low-cost devices that can't run AI at the edge, so they are ripe for replacement," said Mohit Agrawal, Research Director at Counterpoint. "Amazon and Google have only just begun refreshing their hardware for Alexa+ and Gemini, so the upgrade cycle is wide open, and Apple wants to win it."
Apple's $299 price for HomeView is above Amazon's Echo Show 8 at $199.99 and Google's Nest Hub at $99.99, as it seeks a bigger role in connected homes.

The new Apple TV 4K enters the market at $299, more than double the price of its starting price of its predecessor and in line with Nvidia's Shield TV Pro, while rival offerings from Amazon, Google and Roku cost $200 or less.

Shares were up about 1% in Tuesday afternoon trading after earlier touching a record. Apple stock has gained 25% so far this year, outperforming the large-cap Nasdaq 100, which is up 21% for the same period.

extraction.body: NEW YORK, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Apple on Tuesday launched a raft of smart products, including an iPad-like device dubbed the HomeView, in a bet that its AI-upgraded Siri virtual assistant can help it carve out a bigger share of the highly competitive connected home market. The HomeView device, which starts at $299 and starts shipping next month, is Apple's latest entry into a highly competitive market for connected home devices. It will feature a 7-inch screen and face recognition and will help users control doorbells, thermostats and smart locks in a market where Apple has tinkered for a decade without major success. Apple is launching these products as it tries to fend off competition from rivals, including traditional competitors like Amazon.com, which has invested heavily in its Echo speakers and Ring doorbells and last week launched premium tablets, as well as newer AI upstarts like OpenAI that have hardware ambitions of their own. "Apple needs to demonstrate that its AI capabilities can deliver meaningful benefits beyond basic voice commands, simplifying everyday tasks and bringing greater intelligence to the home," said PP Foresight analyst Paolo Pescatore. Investors are looking more closely at Apple's hardware sales for growth. The company's services revenue has come under regulatory pressure, although that could also eventually get a boost from the new suite of devices. "The objective seems to be to drive high-margin 'Services' revenue via Apple TV, Apple Pay and iCloud," said Melissa Otto, head of Visible Alpha Research at S&P Global Market Intelligence, noting that Apple's 2027 services revenue is forecast to rise 12% to $138 billion. "Growth in Apple's lucrative subscription services may be the gateway to earnings growth increases over the next two years." Apple this summer upgraded Siri's capabilities with assistance from Google but analysts said it is unclear whether its AI assistant is competitive enough to lure consumers to a crowded connected home device space. The device features a 7-inch screen — which Apple said is to make it fit into a home without being too imposing — similar to Apple's "sunflower" iMac from the 2000s. And while it features a menu of square app icons like an iPhone or iPad that change depending on which user is recognized, Apple showed it being used more often via voice with its Siri AI assistant. The launches also coincide with growing worries that connected devices, including refrigerators and smart TVs, could be vulnerable to hackers. Apple accompanied the HomeView launch with updates to its HomePod smart speaker and Apple TV devices. It also introduced a range of accessories, including doorbells, cameras and thermostats, made by LG and Schneider Electric and designed with help from Apple. Apple's work with LG and Schneider Electric to sell a suite of products alongside the HomeView was meant to make it easier to add smart home products to a household. Kaiann Drance, Apple's vice president of product marketing for home products, said the devices can be added with a single tap, similar to Apple's first-party devices such as AirPods. "For people who haven't experienced the Home ecosystem or haven't gone further than maybe a product here or there, I think this is a great opportunity to look," Drance told Reuters in an interview. Ben Wood, chief analyst and chief marketing officer for CCS Insight, said that at first glance Apple's partnership with the two outside firms looked like a break with its usual practice of fully controlling its hardware. "However, looking closely, it appears like there has been very deep collaboration between Apple and these partners to ensure the design, engineering and experience closely match what users would expect from Apple," he said. During a video demonstrating the device, Apple showed the HomeView, which is meant to hang on walls or perch on tabletops, and its Siri virtual assistant juggling voice requests from multiple members of a family at the same time. To pull in private data from messages and calendars, the HomeView relies on a user having an iPhone that's been recently unlocked and connected to the same home network. The HomeView device will not be sold in the European Union, because Siri AI remains unavailable there due to EU regulations, Apple said. Apple first released its Home app to control smart gadgets in 2016, with HomePod smart speakers following in 2018, but those offerings are competing with Alphabet's Google Home speakers and Amazon's Echo line. Analysts said two major hurdles for Apple were making its devices work with a variety of third-party gadgets and the limited ability of Siri to give useful answers. “Apple has the brand, technology and loyal customers to make a serious impact, but it is playing catch-up with rivals that have a far stronger presence," Pescatore said. Fragmentation among various companies' "smart" home products and the difficulty of connecting them has proved a hurdle to the market's growth although there is hope that AI-enabled devices from Apple, Google and Amazon could make integration more seamless. "Most smart speakers and hubs in homes today are low-cost devices that can't run AI at the edge, so they are ripe for replacement," said Mohit Agrawal, Research Director at Counterpoint. "Amazon and Google have only just begun refreshing their hardware for Alexa+ and Gemini, so the upgrade cycle is wide open, and Apple wants to win it." Apple's $299 price for HomeView is above Amazon's Echo Show 8 at $199.99 and Google's Nest Hub at $99.99, as it seeks a bigger role in connected homes. The new Apple TV 4K enters the market at $299, more than double the price of its starting price of its predecessor and in line with Nvidia's Shield TV Pro, while rival offerings from Amazon, Google and Roku cost $200 or less. Shares were up about 1% in Tuesday afternoon trading after earlier touching a record. Apple stock has gained 25% so far this year, outperforming the large-cap Nasdaq 100, which is up 21% for the same period. (Reporting by Stephen Nellis in San Francisco; Additional reporting by Anhata Rooprai in Bengaluru; Editing by David Gaffen, Christian Plumb and Aurora Ellis)

Apple this summer upgraded Siri's capabilities with assistance from Google but analysts said it is unclear whether its AI assistant is competitive enough to lure consumers to a crowded connected home device space.

Fragmentation among various companies' "smart" home products and the difficulty of connecting them has proved a hurdle to the market's growth although there is hope that AI-enabled devices from Apple, Google and Amazon could make integration more seamless.

"Apple needs to demonstrate that its AI capabilities can deliver meaningful benefits beyond basic voice commands, simplifying everyday tasks and bringing greater intelligence to the home," said PP Foresight analyst Paolo Pescatore.

"The objective seems to be to drive high-margin 'Services' revenue via Apple TV, Apple Pay and iCloud," said Melissa Otto, head of Visible Alpha Research at S&P Global Market Intelligence, noting that Apple's 2027 services revenue is forecast to rise 12% to $138 billion.
"Growth in Apple's lucrative subscription services may be the gateway to earnings growth increases over the next two years."
"Amazon and Google have only just begun refreshing their hardware for Alexa+ and Gemini, so the upgrade cycle is wide open, and Apple wants to win it."
Investors are looking more closely at Apple's hardware sales for growth.
The company's services revenue has come under regulatory pressure, although that could also eventually get a boost from the new suite of devices.
Apple accompanied the HomeView launch with updates to its HomePod smart speaker and Apple TV devices.
It also introduced a range of accessories, including doorbells, cameras and thermostats, made by LG and Schneider Electric and designed with help from Apple.
Shares were up about 1% in Tuesday afternoon trading after earlier touching a record.
Apple stock has gained 25% so far this year, outperforming the large-cap Nasdaq 100, which is up 21% for the same period.

"However, looking closely, it appears like there has been very deep collaboration between Apple and these partners to ensure the design, engineering and experience closely match what users would expect from Apple," he said.
“Apple has the brand, technology and loyal customers to make a serious impact, but it is playing catch-up with rivals that have a far stronger presence," Pescatore said.

Apple is launching these products as it tries to fend off competition from rivals, including traditional competitors like Amazon.com, which has invested heavily in its Echo speakers and Ring doorbells and last week launched premium tablets, as well as newer AI upstarts like OpenAI that have hardware ambitions of their own.

Ben Wood, chief analyst and chief marketing officer for CCS Insight, said that at first glance Apple's partnership with the two outside firms looked like a break with its usual practice of fully controlling its hardware.
To pull in private data from messages and calendars, the HomeView relies on a user having an iPhone that's been recently unlocked and connected to the same home network.

The announcement was made on October 16, 2026, and Deutsche Bank's crypto custody service is set to expand into Asian financial centers in 2027.

Custody refers to holding private keys, the secret codes that let users manage their cryptocurrencies. Bitcoin and Ether prices barely moved after the news. Bitcoin is trading at approximately $81,497 as of October 17, down 0.7% in the past day, while Ether has dropped 0.8% to around $2,428. Deutsche Bank first announced its custody service on September 16, pledging that European institutional and corporate clients would have access to regulated custody by the end of 2026, pending regulatory approvals. The service will include Bitcoin, Ether, and two stablecoins, USD Coin (CRYPTO:USDC) and EURC (CRYPTO:EURC), linked to the dollar and the euro.

In its latest October update, Deutsche Bank has shortened its timeline, saying the launch is now just weeks away and will focus initially on Germany. Additional services, such as stablecoin offerings, tokenized deposits (which record traditional bank deposits on a blockchain), and digital bonds, will follow, but no specific dates have been set.

This service targets institutions and corporations, so individual account holders will not be able to use it to store cryptocurrencies. It will operate within the corporate bank, which already serves the treasurers and fund managers most likely to seek regulated crypto solutions.

However, Deutsche Bank has not yet shared information about fees, committed client assets, or revenue targets. Custody banks typically charge a small annual fee, so this business model will be sustainable primarily if clients entrust them with significant assets.

BNY ( NYSE:BK ) has pioneered crypto custody, starting services for Bitcoin and Ether in October 2022 after receiving approval from New York's financial regulator. It became the first of the eight U.S. banks deemed systemically important—banks whose failure could impact the wider economy—to safely hold digital currencies.

U.S. Bancorp ( NYSE:USB ) resumed institutional Bitcoin custody in September 2025 after a three-year hiatus, partnering with the crypto firm NYDIG as a sub-custodian. In Europe, both Standard Chartered and BBVA are already offering regulated crypto custody services.

State Street ( NYSE:STT ) launched its Digital Asset Platform on January 15, providing services for tokenized money market funds, ETFs, tokenized deposits, and stablecoins. However, its release does not mention Bitcoin or Ether. Citi has announced plans to introduce crypto custody in 2026, but it has not yet provided a specific launch date.

While bank custody services provide more access to crypto, they do not create new buyers. Custodians hold assets that clients have already chosen to purchase. As of now, Deutsche Bank has not revealed any major clients, committed asset targets, or purchase intentions, so any impact on prices will depend on client usage.

Over the past year, banks and brokers have kept introducing crypto products, yet prices have struggled. For instance, Morgan Stanley launched a spot Bitcoin ETF in April, and Charles Schwab ( NYSE:SCHW ) completed its retail crypto rollout by mid-October, even as Bitcoin fell 23.4% over the year and Ether fell 36.9%.

According to State Street's March regulatory update, regulators have confirmed that banks may provide and outsource crypto custody and execution services. The Basel Committee, which develops global bank capital rules, discussed reviewing its crypto regulations in February, suggesting that easing these standards could make it more financially viable for banks to enter the crypto market.

Client demand may also motivate banks to get involved. Schwab's CEO Rick Wurster noted in July 2025 that clients prefer to keep their investments in one place and want their crypto stored alongside their traditional assets. However, politics may slow banks' adoption of crypto services, as Aaron Cutler warned that crypto firms and those that received regulatory relief could face congressional probes after Democrats won the midterms.

More big banks are likely to follow, as the rules ease and clients ask for it. Deutsche Bank gains a fee business and German institutions gain easier access, but Bitcoin and Ether gain buying pressure only if those institutions place orders. Both coins had also climbed before the news, with Bitcoin up 26.1% and Ether up 26.3% over 60 days, so that rally cannot be credited to a service that has not launched.

For holders, the Deutsche Bank crypto custody launch is solid business news but a weak price signal. If Citi or State Street announces a dated go-live for Bitcoin custody before December 31, the follow-the-leader view gains hard evidence. If Deutsche Bank's German launch arrives without a named client or disclosed assets in custody, it could be plumbing for demand that hasn't shown up yet.

passages: Deutsche Bank is weeks away from letting German institutions park Bitcoin and Ether with a regulated custodian, and the move raises a bigger question: will a wave of bank entries finally translate into lasting price pressure, or just more plumbing…
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

Deutsche Bank ( NYSE:DB | DB Price Prediction ) is just weeks away from providing custody services for Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) and Ether ( CRYPTO:ETH ) to clients in Germany, according to Gerald Podobnik, co-head of the bank’s corporate bank. The announcement was made on October 16, 2026, and Deutsche Bank’s crypto custody service is set to expand into Asian financial centers in 2027.

Custody refers to holding private keys, the secret codes that let users manage their cryptocurrencies. By holding these keys, a bank allows institutions like pension funds or corporate treasuries to own cryptocurrency without needing to handle the keys themselves . For many organizations, partnering with a regulated bank is the only option that meets their compliance requirements.

Bitcoin and Ether prices barely moved after the news. Bitcoin is trading at approximately $81,497 as of October 17, down 0.7% in the past day, while Ether has dropped 0.8% to around $2,428. So, will Deutsche Bank’s move encourage other big banks to follow suit, and could that influx of interest boost these cryptocurrencies’ prices?

Deutsche Bank first announced its custody service on September 16, pledging that European institutional and corporate clients would have access to regulated custody by the end of 2026, pending regulatory approvals. The service will include Bitcoin, Ether, and two stablecoins, USD Coin ( CRYPTO:USDC ) and EURC ( CRYPTO:EURC ), linked to the dollar and the euro.

In its latest October update, Deutsche Bank has shortened its timeline, saying the launch is now just weeks away and will focus initially on Germany. Additional services, such as stablecoin offerings, tokenized deposits (which record traditional bank deposits on a blockchain), and digital bonds, will follow, but no specific dates have been set.

This service targets institutions and corporations, so individual account holders will not be able to use it to store cryptocurrencies. It will operate within the corporate bank, which already serves the treasurers and fund managers most likely to seek regulated crypto solutions.

However, Deutsche Bank has not yet shared information about fees, committed client assets, or revenue targets. Custody banks typically charge a small annual fee, so this business model will be sustainable primarily if clients entrust them with significant assets.

BNY ( NYSE:BK ) has pioneered crypto custody, starting services for Bitcoin and Ether in October 2022 after receiving approval from New York’s financial regulator. It became the first of the eight U.S. banks deemed systemically important—banks whose failure could impact the wider economy—to safely hold digital currencies.

U.S. Bancorp ( NYSE:USB ) resumed institutional Bitcoin custody in September 2025 after a three-year hiatus, partnering with the crypto firm NYDIG as a sub-custodian. In Europe, both Standard Chartered and BBVA are already offering regulated crypto custody services.

State Street ( NYSE:STT ) launched its Digital Asset Platform on January 15, providing services for tokenized money market funds, ETFs, tokenized deposits, and stablecoins. However, its release does not mention Bitcoin or Ether. Citi has announced plans to introduce crypto custody in 2026, but it has not yet provided a specific launch date.

While bank custody services provide more access to crypto, they do not create new buyers. Custodians hold assets that clients have already chosen to purchase. As of now, Deutsche Bank has not revealed any major clients, committed asset targets, or purchase intentions, so any impact on prices will depend on client usage.

Over the past year, banks and brokers have kept introducing crypto products , yet prices have struggled . For instance, Morgan Stanley launched a spot Bitcoin ETF in April, and Charles Schwab ( NYSE:SCHW ) completed its retail crypto rollout by mid-October, even as Bitcoin fell 23.4% over the year and Ether fell 36.9%.

According to State Street’s March regulatory update, regulators have confirmed that banks may provide and outsource crypto custody and execution services. The Basel Committee, which develops global bank capital rules, discussed reviewing its crypto regulations in February, suggesting that easing these standards could make it more financially viable for banks to enter the crypto market.

Client demand may also motivate banks to get involved. Schwab’s CEO Rick Wurster noted in July 2025 that clients prefer to keep their investments in one place and want their crypto stored alongside their traditional assets. However, politics may slow banks’ adoption of crypto services, as Aaron Cutler warned that crypto firms and those that received regulatory relief could face congressional probes after Democrats won the midterms.

More big banks are likely to follow, as the rules ease and clients ask for it. Deutsche Bank gains a fee business and German institutions gain easier access, but Bitcoin and Ether gain buying pressure only if those institutions place orders. Both coins had also climbed before the news, with Bitcoin up 26.1% and Ether up 26.3% over 60 days, so that rally cannot be credited to a service that has not launched.

For holders, the Deutsche Bank crypto custody launch is solid business news but a weak price signal. If Citi or State Street announces a dated go-live for Bitcoin custody before December 31, the follow-the-leader view gains hard evidence. If Deutsche Bank’s German launch arrives without a named client or disclosed assets in custody, it could be plumbing for demand that hasn’t shown up yet.

State Street ( NYSE:STT ) launched its Digital Asset Platform on January 15, providing services for tokenized money market funds, ETFs, tokenized deposits, and stablecoins. However, its release does not mention Bitcoin or Ether. Citi has announced plans to introduce crypto custody in 2026, but it has not yet provided a specific launch date.

While bank custody services provide more access to crypto, they do not create new buyers. Custodians hold assets that clients have already chosen to purchase. As of now, Deutsche Bank has not revealed any major clients, committed asset targets, or purchase intentions, so any impact on prices will depend on client usage.

Over the past year, banks and brokers have kept introducing crypto products , yet prices have struggled . For instance, Morgan Stanley launched a spot Bitcoin ETF in April, and Charles Schwab ( NYSE:SCHW ) completed its retail crypto rollout by mid-October, even as Bitcoin fell 23.4% over the year and Ether fell 36.9%.

According to State Street’s March regulatory update, regulators have confirmed that banks may provide and outsource crypto custody and execution services. The Basel Committee, which develops global bank capital rules, discussed reviewing its crypto regulations in February, suggesting that easing these standards could make it more financially viable for banks to enter the crypto market.

Client demand may also motivate banks to get involved. Schwab’s CEO Rick Wurster noted in July 2025 that clients prefer to keep their investments in one place and want their crypto stored alongside their traditional assets. More big banks are likely to follow, as the rules ease and clients ask for it. Deutsche Bank gains a fee business and German institutions gain easier access, but Bitcoin and Ether gain buying pressure only if those institutions place orders. Both coins had also climbed before the news, with Bitcoin up 26.1% and Ether up 26.3% over 60 days, so that rally cannot be credited to a service that has not launched.

For holders, the Deutsche Bank crypto custody launch is solid business news but a weak price signal. If Citi or State Street announces a dated go-live for Bitcoin custody before December 31, the follow-the-leader view gains hard evidence. If Deutsche Bank’s German launch arrives without a named client or disclosed assets in custody, it could be plumbing for demand that hasn’t shown up yet.

Coinbase Custody serves as the custodian, safeguarding the trust's assets. This means Coinbase holds the private keys—the essential codes that allow access to Bitcoin on the blockchain—in separate accounts to avoid mixing them with other customers' assets. Additionally, Anchorage Digital Bank became a second custodian in April 2025, although BlackRock said at the time it had no plans to transfer any coins there. Authorized participants, large trading firms with contracts to create or redeem shares directly with the trust, are crucial to IBIT's functioning. The structure of ownership doesn't directly affect Bitcoin's price because it doesn't create new demand for the asset.
