Many investors in BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF might think the fund manager owns the Bitcoin. However, the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF ( NASDAQ: IBIT ) has a different structure . While BlackRock ( NYSE: BLK | BLK Price Prediction ) manages the fund, a separate legal trust holds the actual Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ), and Coinbase ( NASDAQ: COIN ) acts as custodian and holds the keys.

IBIT operates as a Delaware statutory trust. Shareholders have beneficial interests in the trust, meaning they benefit from the economic value of the trust’s Bitcoin, but they don’t own the coins outright or can’t withdraw them.

Bitcoin is trading around $81,497 as of October 17, 2026, about 35% below its record high of $126,080 . On October 16, shares of IBIT closed at about $46. So, who owns what, and how does this structure impact Bitcoin’s price?

A Delaware statutory trust is a legal entity that holds assets on behalf of others. In the case of IBIT, this means that the trust holds the legal title to every Bitcoin. So, even though BlackRock manages the ETF, the trust owns the coins.

Shareholders have what are known as beneficial interests—essentially a claim on the trust’s Bitcoin’s economic benefits. As a result, the value of each IBIT share rises and falls with the price of Bitcoin. However, shareholders do not have legal ownership of any specific Bitcoin and cannot withdraw coins directly from the trust.

This structure means that when an investor wants to exit, they must sell their shares on the stock exchange for cash. Long-term shareholders will face limitations if they want to send, spend, or store Bitcoin personally. This setup also keeps Bitcoin separate from BlackRock’s finances, meaning the company cannot list it as part of its corporate treasury or spend it.

BlackRock’s role is to sponsor the ETF. It establishes the trust, hires service providers, manages daily operations, and earns fees for running the ETF. According to an iShares prospectus, BlackRock Fund Advisors and its affiliates managed approximately $13.9 trillion in assets as of March 31, 2026, making IBIT just one of many products under this massive asset manager.

Coinbase Custody serves as the custodian, safeguarding the trust’s assets. This means Coinbase holds the private keys —the essential codes that allow access to Bitcoin on the blockchain—in separate accounts to avoid mixing them with other customers’ assets. Additionally, Anchorage Digital Bank became a second custodian in April 2025, although BlackRock said at the time it had no plans to transfer any coins there.

Authorized participants, large trading firms with contracts to create or redeem shares directly with the trust, are crucial to IBIT’s functioning. Since 2025, these participants can exchange Bitcoin for new shares or return shares to receive Bitcoin in return—ordinary shareholders, however, cannot do this.

The structure of ownership doesn’t directly affect Bitcoin’s price because it doesn’t create new demand for the asset. Instead, the price is influenced by the volume of share creations and redemptions in the ETF.

When demand for IBIT shares exceeds supply, authorized participants can deliver Bitcoin to the trust in exchange for new shares, effectively taking coins off the market. Conversely, heavy selling of IBIT shares can lead to coins being redeemed and returned to traders.

That’s why IBIT closely tracks Bitcoin’s price. Over the past year, IBIT has declined 24.9%, closely mirroring Bitcoin’s 23.4% drop, with the slight difference likely due to fees and different measurement periods.

In summary, the trust owns the Bitcoin, Coinbase Custody secures it, and BlackRock manages everything, while shareholders have a claim on the value of the coins. You can think of an IBIT share as a receipt for Bitcoin stored in someone else’s vault. This arrangement entails some loss of control, as holders depend on all three parties and cannot move the coins themselves.

IBIT is ideal for investors who want to capture Bitcoin’s price movements in a brokerage or retirement account without managing private keys. In contrast, a personal wallet offers direct ownership, but if you lose the seed phrase—the backup words needed to restore access to a wallet—you risk permanently losing your coins. If the trust’s Bitcoin holdings keep growing through November, authorized participants may continue pulling Bitcoin from the market, which could affect overall supply dynamics.

A Delaware statutory trust is a legal entity that holds assets on behalf of others. In the case of IBIT, this means that the trust holds the legal title to every Bitcoin. So, even though BlackRock manages the ETF, the trust owns the coins.

Shareholders have what are known as beneficial interests—essentially a claim on the trust's Bitcoin's economic benefits. As a result, the value of each IBIT share rises and falls with the price of Bitcoin. However, shareholders do not have legal ownership of any specific Bitcoin and cannot withdraw coins directly from the trust.

This structure means that when an investor wants to exit, they must sell their shares on the stock exchange for cash. Long-term shareholders will face limitations if they want to send, spend, or store Bitcoin personally. This setup also keeps Bitcoin separate from BlackRock's finances, meaning the company cannot list it as part of its corporate treasury or spend it.

BlackRock's role is to sponsor the ETF. It establishes the trust, hires service providers, manages daily operations, and earns fees for running the ETF. According to an iShares prospectus, BlackRock Fund Advisors and its affiliates managed approximately $13.9 trillion in assets as of March 31, 2026, making IBIT just one of many products under this massive asset manager.

Coinbase Custody serves as the custodian, safeguarding the trust's assets. This means Coinbase holds the private keys—the essential codes that allow access to Bitcoin on the blockchain—in separate accounts to avoid mixing them with other customers' assets. Additionally, Anchorage Digital Bank became a second custodian in April 2025, although BlackRock said at the time it had no plans to transfer any coins there.

Authorized participants, large trading firms with contracts to create or redeem shares directly with the trust, are crucial to IBIT's functioning. Since 2025, these participants can exchange Bitcoin for new shares or return shares to receive Bitcoin in return—ordinary shareholders, however, cannot do this.

The structure of ownership doesn't directly affect Bitcoin's price because it doesn't create new demand for the asset. Instead, the price is influenced by the volume of share creations and redemptions in the ETF.

When demand for IBIT shares exceeds supply, authorized participants can deliver Bitcoin to the trust in exchange for new shares, effectively taking coins off the market. Conversely, heavy selling of IBIT shares can lead to coins being redeemed and returned to traders.

That's why IBIT closely tracks Bitcoin's price. Over the past year, IBIT has declined 24.9%, closely mirroring Bitcoin's 23.4% drop, with the slight difference likely due to fees and different measurement periods.

In summary, the trust owns the Bitcoin, Coinbase Custody secures it, and BlackRock manages everything, while shareholders have a claim on the value of the coins. You can think of an IBIT share as a receipt for Bitcoin stored in someone else's vault. This arrangement entails some loss of control, as holders depend on all three parties and cannot move the coins themselves.

IBIT is ideal for investors who want to capture Bitcoin's price movements in a brokerage or retirement account without managing private keys. In contrast, a personal wallet offers direct ownership, but if you lose the seed phrase—the backup words needed to restore access to a wallet—you risk permanently losing your coins. In the case of IBIT, this means that the trust holds the legal title to every Bitcoin. So, even though BlackRock manages the ETF, the trust owns the coins. Shareholders have what are known as beneficial interests—essentially a claim on the trust's Bitcoin's economic benefits. As a result, the value of each IBIT share rises and falls with the price of Bitcoin. However, shareholders do not have legal ownership of any specific Bitcoin and cannot withdraw coins directly from the trust. This structure means that when an investor wants to exit, they must sell their shares on the stock exchange for cash. This setup also keeps Bitcoin separate from BlackRock's finances, meaning the company cannot list it as part of its corporate treasury or spend it. BlackRock's role is to sponsor the ETF. It establishes the trust, hires service providers, manages daily operations, and earns fees for running the ETF. According to an iShares prospectus, BlackRock Fund Advisors and its affiliates managed approximately $13.9 trillion in assets as of March 31, 2026, making IBIT just one of many products under this massive asset manager. Coinbase Custody serves as the custodian, safeguarding the trust's assets. This means Coinbase holds the private keys—the essential codes that allow access to Bitcoin on the blockchain—in separate accounts to avoid mixing them with other customers' assets. Additionally, Anchorage Digital Bank became a second custodian in April 2025, although BlackRock said at the time it had no plans to transfer any coins there. Authorized participants, large trading firms with contracts to create or redeem shares directly with the trust, are crucial to IBIT's functioning. Since 2025, these participants can exchange Bitcoin for new shares or return shares to receive Bitcoin in return—ordinary shareholders, however, cannot do this. The structure of ownership doesn't directly affect Bitcoin's price because it doesn't create new demand for the asset. Instead, the price is influenced by the volume of share creations and redemptions in the ETF. When demand for IBIT shares exceeds supply, authorized participants can deliver Bitcoin to the trust in exchange for new shares, effectively taking coins off the market. Conversely, heavy selling of IBIT shares can lead to coins being redeemed and returned to traders. That's why IBIT closely tracks Bitcoin's price. Over the past year, IBIT has declined 24.9%, closely mirroring Bitcoin's 23.4% drop, with the slight difference likely due to fees and different measurement periods. In summary, the trust owns the Bitcoin, Coinbase Custody secures it, and BlackRock manages everything, while shareholders have a claim on the value of the coins. You can think of an IBIT share as a receipt for Bitcoin stored in someone else's vault. This arrangement entails some loss of control, as holders depend on all three parties and cannot move the coins themselves. IBIT is ideal for investors who want to capture Bitcoin's price movements in a brokerage or retirement account without managing private keys. In contrast, a personal wallet offers direct ownership, but if you lose the seed phrase—the backup words needed to restore access to a wallet—you risk permanently losing your coins. If the trust's Bitcoin holdings keep growing through November, authorized participants may continue pulling Bitcoin from the market, which could affect overall supply dynamics. This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

Many investors in BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF might think the fund manager owns the Bitcoin. However, the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF ( NASDAQ: IBIT ) has a different structure . While BlackRock ( NYSE: BLK | BLK Price Prediction ) manages the fund, a separate legal trust holds the actual Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ), and Coinbase ( NASDAQ: COIN ) acts as custodian and holds the keys.

IBIT operates as a Delaware statutory trust. Shareholders have beneficial interests in the trust, meaning they benefit from the economic value of the trust’s Bitcoin, but they don’t own the coins outright or can’t withdraw them.

Bitcoin is trading around $81,497 as of October 17, 2026, about 35% below its record high of $126,080 . On October 16, shares of IBIT closed at about $46. So, who owns what, and how does this structure impact Bitcoin’s price?

A Delaware statutory trust is a legal entity that holds assets on behalf of others. In the case of IBIT, this means that the trust holds the legal title to every Bitcoin. So, even though BlackRock manages the ETF, the trust owns the coins.

Shareholders have what are known as beneficial interests—essentially a claim on the trust’s Bitcoin’s economic benefits. As a result, the value of each IBIT share rises and falls with the price of Bitcoin. However, shareholders do not have legal ownership of any specific Bitcoin and cannot withdraw coins directly from the trust.

This structure means that when an investor wants to exit, they must sell their shares on the stock exchange for cash. Long-term shareholders will face limitations if they want to send, spend, or store Bitcoin personally. This setup also keeps Bitcoin separate from BlackRock’s finances, meaning the company cannot list it as part of its corporate treasury or spend it.

BlackRock’s role is to sponsor the ETF. It establishes the trust, hires service providers, manages daily operations, and earns fees for running the ETF. According to an iShares prospectus, BlackRock Fund Advisors and its affiliates managed approximately $13.9 trillion in assets as of March 31, 2026, making IBIT just one of many products under this massive asset manager.

Coinbase Custody serves as the custodian, safeguarding the trust’s assets. This means Coinbase holds the private keys —the essential codes that allow access to Bitcoin on the blockchain—in separate accounts to avoid mixing them with other customers’ assets. Additionally, Anchorage Digital Bank became a second custodian in April 2025, although BlackRock said at the time it had no plans to transfer any coins there.

Authorized participants, large trading firms with contracts to create or redeem shares directly with the trust, are crucial to IBIT’s functioning. Since 2025, these participants can exchange Bitcoin for new shares or return shares to receive Bitcoin in return—ordinary shareholders, however, cannot do this.

The structure of ownership doesn’t directly affect Bitcoin’s price because it doesn’t create new demand for the asset. Instead, the price is influenced by the volume of share creations and redemptions in the ETF.

When demand for IBIT shares exceeds supply, authorized participants can deliver Bitcoin to the trust in exchange for new shares, effectively taking coins off the market. Conversely, heavy selling of IBIT shares can lead to coins being redeemed and returned to traders.

That’s why IBIT closely tracks Bitcoin’s price. Over the past year, IBIT has declined 24.9%, closely mirroring Bitcoin’s 23.4% drop, with the slight difference likely due to fees and different measurement periods.

In summary, the trust owns the Bitcoin, Coinbase Custody secures it, and BlackRock manages everything, while shareholders have a claim on the value of the coins. You can think of an IBIT share as a receipt for Bitcoin stored in someone else’s vault. This arrangement entails some loss of control, as holders depend on all three parties and cannot move the coins themselves.

IBIT is ideal for investors who want to capture Bitcoin’s price movements in a brokerage or retirement account without managing private keys. In contrast, a personal wallet offers direct ownership, but if you lose the seed phrase—the backup words needed to restore access to a wallet—you risk permanently losing your coins. If the trust’s Bitcoin holdings keep growing through November, authorized participants may continue pulling Bitcoin from the market, which could affect overall supply dynamics.

Fundstrat co-founder Tom Lee described the cryptocurrency market as “a coiled spring.” He believes that while prices have dipped, the reasons to invest in these assets remain strong. A coiled spring holds energy when compressed, and Lee sees the latest crypto pullback as a similar situation.

Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) is trading at about $81,497, down 3.6% over the past two weeks but up 7.8% over the last 30 days. Bitcoin hit the lower end of its trading range on October 14 after investors grew more cautious.
So, which major coins have pulled back the most, and which declines might be a temporary pause in an upward trend?

Lee compares cryptocurrencies to chip stocks and AI cloud companies, suggesting that all three are like a coiled spring if their underlying fundamentals remain sound. He notes that these assets have “pulled back to support levels.” A support level is a price point where previous buyers stepped in, often stalling price declines.

Lee emphasizes that when strong fundamentals persist and market sentiment turns sour, investors get a favorable risk-reward scenario. This means the potential upside outweighs the possible downsides. Market fear can quickly drive prices down, creating a buying opportunity for those with a more optimistic view.

Fundstrat strategist Mark Newton has taken this analysis a step further, suggesting the market could bottom out within a few days. While Lee did not specify a price target for any coin, he has suggested that Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) is nearing the end of its prolonged decline against Bitcoin .

Among the top coins, Hedera ( CRYPTO:HBAR ) has seen the largest decline, dropping 17.8% in the last two weeks. This pullback follows a substantial 27% jump after an IBM cloud announcement on September 28. The table below shows prices as of October 16, including Bitcoin and Ethereum for comparison.

All seven coins in this analysis lost value over the past 24 hours, with smaller coins typically showing steeper declines during a pullback. Bitcoin’s relatively mild 3.6% two-week drop stands out compared to the larger decreases observed in Uniswap ( CRYPTO:UNI ), Stellar ( CRYPTO:XLM ), Litecoin ( CRYPTO:LTC ), and Aave ( CRYPTO:AAVE ).
Despite these pullbacks, all seven coins posted positive returns over the past 30 days, as most losses followed a strong price surge from September into October.

Aave, a lending protocol that facilitates borrowing and lending of cryptocurrencies, displays a chart that most suggests a reset. The coin fell 13.5% over the past two weeks but remains up 32.5% over 30 days, indicating that this drop is likely profit-taking during an upward trend.
Litecoin, Hedera, and Uniswap show similar patterns; each has given back only part of its monthly gains, with Litecoin up 17.1%, Hedera 14.9%, and Uniswap 14.3%.
Conversely, Stellar appears to have a weaker outlook. XLM has dropped 15.3% over two weeks and has only gained 1.0% this month, trading 79.4% below its all-time high of $0.88 in January 2018.

Ethereum mirrors this trend, with little room left to run, posting a 1.3% monthly gain and trading 51.1% below its previous peak of $4,946 from August 2025. Bitcoin is also well below its high, down 35.4% from its October 2025 record of $126,080 .

In the current crypto pullback, Lee’s description seems to fit Aave, Litecoin, Hedera, and Uniswap more than Stellar or Ethereum. In contrast, Stellar and Ethereum show diminishing momentum, indicating their drops might signal a weakening trend.

The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), a major player in settling U.S. stock trades, expects Stellar (CRYPTO:XLM) to join its upcoming Tokenization Service in 2027, according to its roadmap.

Stellar will not be part of the October launch, and DTCC has not confirmed a specific date for its entry.
Ethereum significantly outpaces Stellar in tokenized assets, with $17 billion in tokenized RWAs and $147.1 billion in stablecoins.
However, Ethereum has already attracted substantial institutional investment that Stellar still needs to secure.

The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), a major player in settling U.S. stock trades, expects Stellar (CRYPTO:XLM) to join its upcoming Tokenization Service in 2027, according to its roadmap. Tokenization converts stocks and bonds into digital tokens that can be traded on a blockchain. With this news, XLM is back on buyers' radar, especially after a 15.3% decline over the past two weeks. XLM is trading at approximately $0.18, down 0.6% in the last 24 hours. By comparison, Ethereum (CRYPTO:ETH) trades around $2,417 and plays a major role in the tokenized asset market, though its connection to DTCC's upcoming service is less direct. So, in the XLM vs Ethereum debate, which cryptocurrency stands as the better investment to capitalize on the tokenization trend? DTCC plans to launch its Tokenization Service in October on two platforms, Canton Network and Besu, its private network. Canton is designed for financial institutions such as banks and asset managers, ensuring trade details remain confidential among the parties involved. The initial rollout will cover 25 stocks, ETFs, and U.S. Treasuries, with each token fully backed by a corresponding security held at the Depository Trust Company (DTC), a DTCC subsidiary. Token holders will have the flexibility to transfer their tokens at any time between registered wallets. DTCC estimates it will have around $30 trillion in assets available for tokenization. Before the official launch, DTCC conducted a successful test on July 15, turning DTC-held securities into tokens for live trades on both Besu and Canton, involving more than 30 participating firms. DTCC has described this initiative as part of a "multi-chain strategy" to ensure resiliency, scalability, and choice for users. While DTCC's roadmap indicates a potential inclusion for Stellar and the Arc network in 2027, this plan is subject to change. Stellar will not be part of the October launch, and DTCC has not confirmed a specific date for its entry. Stellar has already made strides in this space, managing $3.6 billion in tokenized real-world assets (excluding stablecoins), ranking fourth among all networks, according to rwa.xyz data from October 17. These real-world assets (RWAs) include tokenized Treasury funds and private credit. However, despite its accomplishments, XLM's price does not reflect this progress well. XLM trades 79.6% below its January 2018 peak of $0.88 and has fallen 41.4% over the past year. XLM's supply also puts pressure on its price. Approximately 35.2 billion of 50 billion XLM tokens are in circulation, giving a fully diluted valuation (the value if all tokens were in circulation) of about $8.9 billion, compared with a market cap of around $6.3 billion. This indicates that more tokens could be released into the market, potentially absorbing new demand. The connection between Ethereum and DTCC comes through Besu, an Ethereum client, meaning DTCC's private network uses Ethereum technology but operates separately from the public Ethereum blockchain. Ethereum significantly outpaces Stellar in tokenized assets, with $17 billion in tokenized RWAs and $147.1 billion in stablecoins. In contrast, Stellar holds only $535 million in stablecoins, according to the same data source. Price performance has also favored Ethereum. ETH trades 51.1% below its record high of $4,946 from August 2025 and is up 29.3% over the past 90 days, while XLM has dropped 3.8%. Over the last two weeks, ETH fell 9.3%, while XLM fell more sharply, down 15.3%. One advantage XLM has is its smaller market cap, with Ethereum's $295.2 billion about 47 times larger. Smaller cryptocurrencies can often react more sharply to news from large partners. However, Ethereum has already attracted substantial institutional investment that Stellar still needs to secure. In the XLM vs Ethereum comparison, Ethereum stands as the more reliable choice for investors interested in tokenization. DTCC's 2027 roadmap doesn't change that. Investors considering XLM face significant risk from a potential DTCC catalyst that is still a year away and could change. For XLM to narrow the gap, DTCC's October launch needs to progress smoothly, Stellar's rollout date must be confirmed, and its tokenized asset base should keep growing. DTCC plans to launch its Tokenization Service in October on two platforms, Canton Network and Besu, its private network. Canton is designed for financial institutions such as banks and asset managers, ensuring trade details remain confidential among the parties involved.

The initial rollout will cover 25 stocks, ETFs, and U.S. Treasuries, with each token fully backed by a corresponding security held at the Depository Trust Company (DTC), a DTCC subsidiary. Stellar has already made strides in this space, managing $3.6 billion in tokenized real-world assets (excluding stablecoins), ranking fourth among all networks, according to rwa.xyz data from October 17. These real-world assets (RWAs) include tokenized Treasury funds and private credit.
However, despite its accomplishments, XLM's price does not reflect this progress well. XLM trades 79.6% below its January 2018 peak of $0.88 and has fallen 41.4% over the past year.

XLM's supply also puts pressure on its price. Approximately 35.2 billion of 50 billion XLM tokens are in circulation, giving a fully diluted valuation (the value if all tokens were in circulation) of about $8.9 billion, compared with a market cap of around $6.3 billion. This indicates that more tokens could be released into the market, potentially absorbing new demand.
The connection between Ethereum and DTCC comes through Besu, an Ethereum client, meaning DTCC's private network uses Ethereum technology but operates separately from the public Ethereum blockchain.

Ethereum significantly outpaces Stellar in tokenized assets, with $17 billion in tokenized RWAs and $147.1 billion in stablecoins. In contrast, Stellar holds only $535 million in stablecoins, according to the same data source.

In the XLM vs Ethereum comparison, Ethereum stands as the more reliable choice for investors interested in tokenization. DTCC's 2027 roadmap doesn't change that. Investors considering XLM face significant risk from a potential DTCC catalyst that is still a year away and could change. For XLM to narrow the gap, DTCC's October launch needs to progress smoothly, Stellar's rollout date must be confirmed, and its tokenized asset base should keep growing.

Technically, XLM must first recover to $0.20, roughly 12% above its current price and a level it held on October 10. sources.body: This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal. AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday. extraction.body: AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday. The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it had received “multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers” whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, “had reached the live systems of Indian organizations.” The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles, and their actions “exceeded the authorisation of their assigned tasks.” This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal. At Hugging Face, OpenAI’s agents started the same way but then found and exploited software flaws to run code on the company’s servers. CERT-In described no such hacking in India, where the agents appear to have simply used the access left lying around. Still, the Indian cases appear to be worse in one respect, which is what the agents saw: In Australia, OpenAI said it found no evidence its agents touched individuals’ medical or criminal records, even after they wrote files inside a Medicare statistics system, while in India, agents read personal data and confidential business records. And unlike earlier incidents, each disclosed by a single lab, India’s case involved agents from multiple providers. CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations, or say whether the agents altered any systems. TechCrunch has reached out to CERT-In for more information. For now, the closest parallel seems to be Anthropic’s July disclosure of Claude breaking into three companies’ systems during testing using basic techniques like weak passwords. In India, as in Anthropic’s cases, the affected organizations had not detected the intrusions on their own. The disclosures have left governments relying on AI companies causing these breaches to voluntarily disclose rogue AI agent activity. The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it had received “multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers” whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, “had reached the live systems of Indian organizations.”

The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles, and their actions “exceeded the authorisation of their assigned tasks.”

This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal.

At Hugging Face, OpenAI’s agents started the same way but then found and exploited software flaws to run code on the company’s servers. CERT-In described no such hacking in India, where the agents appear to have simply used the access left lying around.

Still, the Indian cases appear to be worse in one respect, which is what the agents saw: In Australia, OpenAI said it found no evidence its agents touched individuals’ medical or criminal records, even after they wrote files inside a Medicare statistics system, while in India, agents read personal data and confidential business records. And unlike earlier incidents, each disclosed by a single lab, India’s case involved agents from multiple providers.
CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations, or say whether the agents altered any systems. TechCrunch has reached out to CERT-In for more information.
For now, the closest parallel seems to be Anthropic’s July disclosure of Claude breaking into three companies’ systems during testing using basic techniques like weak passwords.

In India, as in Anthropic’s cases, the affected organizations had not detected the intrusions on their own. The disclosures have left governments relying on AI companies causing these breaches to voluntarily disclose rogue AI agent activity.

sources.title: Apple’s HomeView is just the latest threat to online recipe writers
passages: Saxena says that for established writers, this is “more like a continuation of the threats they’ve already seen.” Unless Apple sells vast quantities of HomeView displays, its recipe function is still likely to be used by far fewer people than Google’s AI search recipes, let alone recipes from other AI assistants and tools, which are also more egregious in how they take advantage of online content.

The problem is that converting a recipe into easy-to-follow instructions in Apple’s own format also strips it of its context, including the ads and affiliate links that many recipe writers rely on for their income.
Apple’s approach, which it says will work with any online recipe that uses Google’s search-friendly recipe formatting, is unique among the current smart home hubs.
I’ve asked Apple how the HomeView recipe tool will handle paywalled recipes, but at the time of publishing haven’t gotten an answer.
Recipes may often be free to read, but they’re not free to create, and solutions like Apple’s remove the main ways websites and writers recoup those costs.

Apple’s new smart display sits in the center of the chaos on the kitchen table, helping the family check their calendars, send messages, and pull up a French toast recipe in seconds, with simple, step-by-step instructions.
“Recipe writers needed to pad out the text in a certain way so that their recipes would have a chance of coming up in a Google search,” Makalintal explains.
To load a recipe onto the HomeView screen you have to first open it either on your iPhone or through Safari on the HomeView itself, ensuring you’ll see its ads at least once.
Amazon’s Echo Show displays offer similar hands-free cooking features to the HomeView’s, though only with partner sites like Allrecipes or Epicurious.

“I would put the threat level below AI summaries,” says Makalintal, because their “opaque” sourcing “really is erasing labor.” Some major recipe platforms might be able to reduce the impact by getting on board.
There’s only one group of people likely to object: the food writers who created those recipes in the first place.
For one thing, it’s usually the only part of a recipe that a writer can copyright — the rest is regarded as mere instructions.

Perhaps most egregious of all, Google Search now uses Gemini AI to amalgamate online recipes, presenting a streamlined version right on the search page, saving users from ever needing to click through to the original sources at all.

extraction.body: When Apple revealed the HomeView to the world, it did so with an unusual ad for the company: Instead of pristine, polished tech in immaculate rooms, it’s a three-minute look at the messy, frantic morning routine of a family of five. Apple’s new smart display sits in the center of the chaos on the kitchen table, helping the family check their calendars, send messages, and pull up a French toast recipe in seconds, with simple, step-by-step instructions. The HomeView is just the latest in a long line of websites, browser extensions, and smart home gadgets with the same promise: that it can take an online recipe and strip it down to the essentials. Instead of scrolling a lengthy webpage that might range from helpful cooking instructions to seemingly irrelevant personal anecdotes, with the recipe itself way down at the bottom, you simply get ingredient lists, cooking instructions, and timers, all navigable hands-free with voice controls and Siri AI. There’s only one group of people likely to object: the food writers who created those recipes in the first place. I would know, since I’m one of them — I have my own food newsletter where I occasionally publish recipes, so I have a little skin in the game. The problem is that converting a recipe into easy-to-follow instructions in Apple’s own format also strips it of its context, including the ads and affiliate links that many recipe writers rely on for their income. Recipes may often be free to read, but they’re not free to create, and solutions like Apple’s remove the main ways websites and writers recoup those costs. Behemoths like Allrecipes and NYT Cooking host tens of thousands of recipes each, some from professional chefs and others from home cooks. Countless dedicated food publications run original recipe content, and thousands of independent chefs produce their own, across blogs, newsletters, YouTube accounts, and TikTok pages. While much of the writing on a recipe page may get on budding cooks’ nerves — we’ve all heard the jokes about being forced to read someone’s grandma’s life story before getting to their cookie recipe — it’s there for a reason. For one thing, it’s usually the only part of a recipe that a writer can copyright — the rest is regarded as mere instructions. But that extra writing is also there because before it worked so hard to strip the text out, Big Tech insisted on it. “Recipe writers needed to pad out the text in a certain way so that their recipes would have a chance of coming up in a Google search,” Makalintal explains. The good news for recipe writers is that Apple’s approach guarantees at least one visit to their original web page. To load a recipe onto the HomeView screen you have to first open it either on your iPhone or through Safari on the HomeView itself, ensuring you’ll see its ads at least once. "“Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll. So if you’re still out here complaining about these essays, you’re just an asshole.”" - Jaya Saxena It’s not just bad for the writers, either — readers and home cooks may be missing out too. “The additional information around recipes can sometimes be really helpful when it comes to troubleshooting problems that could come up while cooking or addressing things like ingredient swaps,” says Makalintal. Apple’s simplified steps may make some recipes easier to follow, but others might become harder without crucial context included elsewhere on the page. And as common as gripes about recipe intros are, they’ve long been easy to skip if you really insist. “Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll,” says Jaya Saxena, one of the founder-owners of the food website Ravenous. In 2021 startup Recipeasly promised to “fix” online recipes by removing the ads and “life stories.” It barely lasted a weekend before online backlash forced its founders to take it offline. Amazon’s Echo Show displays offer similar hands-free cooking features to the HomeView’s, though only with partner sites like Allrecipes or Epicurious. Google’s Nest Hubs used to as well, though Google ultimately removed the step-by-step recipe feature from its Nest Hubs in 2024, along with other “underutilized” features. Apple’s approach, which it says will work with any online recipe that uses Google’s search-friendly recipe formatting, is unique among the current smart home hubs. Perhaps most egregious of all, Google Search now uses Gemini AI to amalgamate online recipes, presenting a streamlined version right on the search page, saving users from ever needing to click through to the original sources at all. Saxena says that for established writers, this is “more like a continuation of the threats they’ve already seen.” Unless Apple sells vast quantities of HomeView displays, its recipe function is still likely to be used by far fewer people than Google’s AI search recipes, let alone recipes from other AI assistants and tools, which are also more egregious in how they take advantage of online content. “I would put the threat level below AI summaries,” says Makalintal, because their “opaque” sourcing “really is erasing labor.” Some major recipe platforms might be able to reduce the impact by getting on board. While the HomeView doesn’t have its own app store, it does support casting apps to the screen using the same tech as CarPlay. That means big apps like Allrecipes or NYT Cooking will have the option of presenting content on the HomeView on their own terms. Independent writers are unlikely to be able to do the same. Smaller recipe developers are turning to Substack, says Makalintal, where it’s easy to lock recipes behind a paywall. I’m one of them — on my newsletter I restrict my recipes to paid subscribers, a reflection of the fact that they’re the most time-consuming articles I publish. I’ve asked Apple how the HomeView recipe tool will handle paywalled recipes, but at the time of publishing haven’t gotten an answer. But the move en masse to newsletter platforms “has led to some subscription fatigue among home cooks,” Makalintal says, and few cooks will start a paid subscription to access a single recipe, suggesting it’s not likely to support the whole industry.

extraction.body: When Apple revealed the HomeView to the world, it did so with an unusual ad for the company: Instead of pristine, polished tech in immaculate rooms, it’s a three-minute look at the messy, frantic morning routine of a family of five. Apple’s new smart display sits in the center of the chaos on the kitchen table, helping the family check their calendars, send messages, and pull up a French toast recipe in seconds, with simple, step-by-step instructions. The HomeView is just the latest in a long line of websites, browser extensions, and smart home gadgets with the same promise: that it can take an online recipe and strip it down to the essentials. Instead of scrolling a lengthy webpage that might range from helpful cooking instructions to seemingly irrelevant personal anecdotes, with the recipe itself way down at the bottom, you simply get ingredient lists, cooking instructions, and timers, all navigable hands-free with voice controls and Siri AI. There’s only one group of people likely to object: the food writers who created those recipes in the first place. I would know, since I’m one of them — I have my own food newsletter where I occasionally publish recipes, so I have a little skin in the game. The problem is that converting a recipe into easy-to-follow instructions in Apple’s own format also strips it of its context, including the ads and affiliate links that many recipe writers rely on for their income. Recipes may often be free to read, but they’re not free to create, and solutions like Apple’s remove the main ways websites and writers recoup those costs. Behemoths like Allrecipes and NYT Cooking host tens of thousands of recipes each, some from professional chefs and others from home cooks. Countless dedicated food publications run original recipe content, and thousands of independent chefs produce their own, across blogs, newsletters, YouTube accounts, and TikTok pages. While much of the writing on a recipe page may get on budding cooks’ nerves — we’ve all heard the jokes about being forced to read someone’s grandma’s life story before getting to their cookie recipe — it’s there for a reason. For one thing, it’s usually the only part of a recipe that a writer can copyright — the rest is regarded as mere instructions. But that extra writing is also there because before it worked so hard to strip the text out, Big Tech insisted on it. “Recipe writers needed to pad out the text in a certain way so that their recipes would have a chance of coming up in a Google search,” Makalintal explains. The good news for recipe writers is that Apple’s approach guarantees at least one visit to their original web page. To load a recipe onto the HomeView screen you have to first open it either on your iPhone or through Safari on the HomeView itself, ensuring you’ll see its ads at least once. "“Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll. So if you’re still out here complaining about these essays, you’re just an asshole.”" - Jaya Saxena It’s not just bad for the writers, either — readers and home cooks may be missing out too. “The additional information around recipes can sometimes be really helpful when it comes to troubleshooting problems that could come up while cooking or addressing things like ingredient swaps,” says Makalintal. Apple’s simplified steps may make some recipes easier to follow, but others might become harder without crucial context included elsewhere on the page. And as common as gripes about recipe intros are, they’ve long been easy to skip if you really insist. “Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll,” says Jaya Saxena, one of the founder-owners of the food website Ravenous. In 2021 startup Recipeasly promised to “fix” online recipes by removing the ads and “life stories.” It barely lasted a weekend before online backlash forced its founders to take it offline. Amazon’s Echo Show displays offer similar hands-free cooking features to the HomeView’s, though only with partner sites like Allrecipes or Epicurious. Google’s Nest Hubs used to as well, though Google ultimately removed the step-by-step recipe feature from its Nest Hubs in 2024, along with other “underutilized” features. Apple’s approach, which it says will work with any online recipe that uses Google’s search-friendly recipe formatting, is unique among the current smart home hubs. Perhaps most egregious of all, Google Search now uses Gemini AI to amalgamate online recipes, presenting a streamlined version right on the search page, saving users from ever needing to click through to the original sources at all. Saxena says that for established writers, this is “more like a continuation of the threats they’ve already seen.” Unless Apple sells vast quantities of HomeView displays, its recipe function is still likely to be used by far fewer people than Google’s AI search recipes, let alone recipes from other AI assistants and tools, which are also more egregious in how they take advantage of online content. “I would put the threat level below AI summaries,” says Makalintal, because their “opaque” sourcing “really is erasing labor.” Some major recipe platforms might be able to reduce the impact by getting on board. While the HomeView doesn’t have its own app store, it does support casting apps to the screen using the same tech as CarPlay. That means big apps like Allrecipes or NYT Cooking will have the option of presenting content on the HomeView on their own terms. Independent writers are unlikely to be able to do the same. Smaller recipe developers are turning to Substack, says Makalintal, where it’s easy to lock recipes behind a paywall. I’m one of them — on my newsletter I restrict my recipes to paid subscribers, a reflection of the fact that they’re the most time-consuming articles I publish. I’ve asked Apple how the HomeView recipe tool will handle paywalled recipes, but at the time of publishing haven’t gotten an answer. But the move en masse to newsletter platforms “has led to some subscription fatigue among home cooks,” Makalintal says, and few cooks will start a paid subscription to access a single recipe, suggesting it’s not likely to support the whole industry.

sources.title: Don’t Let a Crypto Inheritance Get Stuck on the Blockchain

extraction.body: In the US, cryptocurrency is considered a digital asset rather than money in terms of probate and estate law. With digital assets, however, the law says we should not assume that a deceased person wanted their private materials—everything from emails to photos—given to another person unless they explicitly said so. This puts cryptocurrency, as a digital asset, in an awkward position. The options for arranging a transfer of cryptocurrency upon one's death or incapacitation breaks down by one big division: whether the crypto is held by a custodian or in a noncustodial crypto wallet. Two Types of Wallets A custodian or custodial wallet means a third party, such as a bank or a cryptocurrency marketplace, holds and manages the assets for you. For crypto enthusiasts whose interest in digital currency is driven by a distaste for the traditional banking system, then using a noncustodial wallet is kind of the whole point. It can even be a piece of paper with the instructions and passwords for accessing the cryptocurrency on it. (I use "password" here and throughout to refer to any string of letters, numbers, and characters needed to gain access to someone’s cryptocurrency.) Whatever kind of noncustodial wallet you choose, passing on your assets will require a DIY solution. Pros and Cons of a Custodial Wallet When you use a third-party custodian to hold your cryptocurrency, you can choose one that has a beneficiary process in place. Charles Schwab and Chase are just two examples of large, well-known financial institutions that offer crypto services and have experience transferring assets after death. Schwab, for example, houses its cryptocurrency services within brokerage accounts. Signing a beneficiary form for a brokerage account applies to the crypto account as well. Another benefit of using a bank is that at least three entities know you have an account: the bank, the government, and the credit reporting bureaus. More important to your heirs, it doesn't matter if you were locked out of the online portal when you died—that has no bearing on the account or a beneficiary's ability to receive the funds. Note that cryptocurrency accounts, even when held through a bank, are not FDIC-insured. Other custodians include crypto marketplaces, such as Coinbase, and peer-to-peer payment services, like PayPal. Neither Coinbase nor PayPal have beneficiary forms as of this writing, though they do have a clear process for proving a person is entitled to a decedent's account. In both cases, you must have legal documents saying you are the executor of the estate (for PayPal) or are entitled to inherit the account (Coinbase), as well as a death certificate and other documentation. As mentioned, crypto enthusiasts who eschew traditional banking may not see any value in using a custodian. Banks require ID, so you cannot hold the crypto anonymously. Banks and many other custodians report your transactions to the federal government, holding you accountable to an honest tax filing. sources.title: Mark Wahlberg on using AI in film ‘the right way’ and being open to an AI clone carrying on his legacy
passages: Wahlberg, who’s also an entrepreneur and angel investor, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt to share his perspective on AI’s role in filmmaking, and how he’s open to having an AI likeness of himself carry on his legacy.
Even as Hollywood remains divided over the use of AI in filmmaking, actor and director Mark Wahlberg believes the technology has a place in the industry as long as it’s used the right way.

“It’s a fairly expensive movie, but, we’re talking about utilizing [AI] to enhance the stadium setting, things of that nature,” Wahlberg said. “I don’t think you should just, you know, put an idea into ChatGPT and it puts out a script, and then you should go make that and not use real actors.
Those are cutting-edge moments in technology with computer-generated images.
He even said he wouldn’t be opposed if his upcoming animated series, “Ted,” continued for decades with an AI version of his likeness.

When asked by TechCrunch Editor-in-Chief Connie Loizos whether he had visited the CAA Vault , a Creative Artists Agency facility which lets actors use scanning technology to capture their bodies, faces, movements, and voices to create AI replicas, Wahlberg said he hadn’t, but would be open to the idea.

“It’s a fairly expensive movie, but, we’re talking about utilizing [AI] to enhance the stadium setting, things of that nature,” Wahlberg said. “I don’t think you should just, you know, put an idea into ChatGPT and it puts out a script, and then you should go make that and not use real actors.
Those are cutting-edge moments in technology with computer-generated images.
He even said he wouldn’t be opposed if his upcoming animated series, “Ted,” continued for decades with an AI version of his likeness.

When asked by TechCrunch Editor-in-Chief Connie Loizos whether he had visited the CAA Vault , a Creative Artists Agency facility which lets actors use scanning technology to capture their bodies, faces, movements, and voices to create AI replicas, Wahlberg said he hadn’t, but would be open to the idea.

The actor said he plans to potentially use AI to enhance certain aspects of the upcoming Pete Rose biopic, in which he’ll star in the title role. “It’s a fairly expensive movie, but, we’re talking about utilizing [AI] to enhance the stadium setting, things of that nature,” Wahlberg said. “I don’t think you should just, you know, put an idea into ChatGPT and it puts out a script, and then you should go make that and not use real actors. Now, I think it’s hard to do that, so I’m not so passionate about effects-driven movies per se, as opposed to real storytelling.” When asked by TechCrunch Editor-in-Chief Connie Loizos whether he had visited the CAA Vault , a Creative Artists Agency facility which lets actors use scanning technology to capture their bodies, faces, movements, and voices to create AI replicas, Wahlberg said he hadn’t, but would be open to the idea. “I would be interested because I think in the future, if that’s where things go, it would be cool that my children or my grandchildren could be in charge of my likeness and my image, and hopefully put me in some good movies,” Wahlberg said. “It’ll be interesting to see where things go.” He even said he wouldn’t be opposed if his upcoming animated series, “Ted,” continued for decades with an AI version of his likeness. “I think it’s cool if I’m no longer able to do it or don’t exist, and if it could continue and people want to see it, I think it’d be interesting to see where things go,” Wahlberg said. “I think there’s certain things from my childhood that I wish still existed and were still a part of my life […] I wouldn’t be opposed to it. passages: Russia is establishing a “security zone” inside Ukraine along the border and it will be non-negotiable in any ⁠future talks with Kyiv, Vladimir Putin has said .

The Russian president, wearing military uniform and speaking during a visit to a command post, said the operation ⁠was in response to Ukraine’s ⁠2024-25 incursion into ​Russia’s western Kursk region .
This task is being carried out successfully,” he said in televised comments on Friday.
“Our goal is to ensure the absolute security of Russia’s border regions ⁠for the future, and we do not plan to make this a subject for potential peace negotiations with ​Ukraine.”
The planned ‌security zone spanned 660km (410 ‌miles) , of which 70% was currently under Russia’s control, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said.
Peskov did not say how deep it would ‌reach inside Ukraine.
The zone requires Russia to carve out land in the Sumy and Kharkiv regions, which are not among those it is illegally claiming as its own territory.

Zelenskyy said the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service had not yet been fully restored , as media reports suggested the order to throttle the service had come from within the White House.
Zelenskyy met European leaders on Friday in Brussels and asked the EU for another €70bn ($79bn/£59bn) next year to fund Ukraine’s defence against Russia, report Jennifer Rankin and Andrew Roth .
Hours earlier Trump called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” after his purported “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold.
The attacks came as a new report showed that civilian casualties from Russia’s invasion have climbed steeply.
At least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 wounded last month – a total that is 85% higher than in September last year, the report from the UN human rights office in Kyiv said on Friday.
It said intensifying Russian attacks in October already had killed dozens of civilians, including children.
“The first two weeks of October were among the deadliest periods for civilians in years,” said Danielle Bell, the UN office head.

As Russian missiles and drones have systematically slammed into power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv this week, the rolling blackouts and water outages have increasingly resembled a supposed Russian blueprint to destroy life in major Ukrainian cities seen by the Guardian, writes Andrew Roth in this analysis .
Two were kiled and 12 more wounded in attacks on three districts of the eastern city of Kharkiv, governor Oleh Syniehubov ⁠said.
Further Russian strikes through the evening injured nine, officials said.
A Russian ⁠airstrike on ​Kherson in southern ⁠Ukraine killed one ⁠person ​and ‌injured ‌19 others , the governor ‌said on Saturday.
The person ‌killed was an ​ambulance driver and ⁠a child ​was among the ​injured, ​Oleksandr Prokudin ​said ‌on ​Telegram.

passages: If you own a Samsung Galaxy phone running One UI 6.0 or later, you may have a built-in security feature called Auto Blocker working in the background without even realizing it.
Epic Games even filed a lawsuit against Samsung a couple of years ago, arguing that this very feature made downloading third-party apps unnecessarily difficult.
Its main job is to stop app installation from outside the Google Play Store or Samsung's Galaxy Store, efficiently closing off one of the most common ways malware ends up on a phone.
Beyond that, Auto Blocker filters images suspected of containing malicious code in messaging apps like Samsung Messages, Google Messages, Messenger, WhatsApp or Telegram.
You'll need to authenticate before switching it off, which is a great feature that can protect you if someone gets their hands on your phone and tries to install some malware.

For users who want even stronger protections, Samsung offers another mode called "Maximum restrictions," which adds extra safeguards, such as blocking device admin apps and work profiles, disabling 2G network connections, preventing auto-reconnection to unsecured Wi-Fi and stripping location data from shared photos.
The feature is efficient in guarding against malicious apps, unauthorized USB access and tampered software updates; threats that are easy to overlook until something goes wrong.

extraction.body: Samsung's Auto Blocker keeps threats at bay, but it can also get in your way. If you own a Samsung Galaxy phone running One UI 6.0 or later, you may have a built-in security feature called Auto Blocker working in the background without even realizing it. Enabled by default on devices that ship with One UI 6.1.1 or later, it filters out apps, USB commands and messages that could put your device at risk without you even having to lift a finger. For most people, that's a super useful layer of protection in a world where threats are extremely common and can come from apps, a public charging cable or images you get in a text. But Auto Blocker isn't without its complications, especially for users who like to sideload apps, work with developer tools or install software from outside the Google Play Store or the Samsung Galaxy Store. Epic Games even filed a lawsuit against Samsung a couple of years ago, arguing that this very feature made downloading third-party apps unnecessarily difficult. Understanding what Auto Blocker actually does and what it doesn't can help you make a smarter decision about whether to keep it on, turn it off or somewhere in between. Let's see what this feature does, how you can enable or disable it and what's the best thing to do. Auto Blocker is a built-in security feature available on Galaxy devices using One UI 6 or higher. Its main job is to stop app installation from outside the Google Play Store or Samsung's Galaxy Store, efficiently closing off one of the most common ways malware ends up on a phone. OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts. The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own. The incident—which likely would have resulted in criminal charges had they been performed directly by a person—has further heightened concerns that widespread AI use could have harmful effects on an unprecedented scale. In two of the cases reported Thursday, OpenAI agents tasked with retrieving information from websites hacked them when the models ran into obstacles obtaining it directly. In one incident during reinforcement training, a model that received access denials when trying to retrieve historical hospital-bed statistics on a government statistics website “used the site’s file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials,” OpenAI said . “It inspected the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint’s authorization checks, and retrieved data that had previously been denied. The model saved the data locally.” In the other incident , a model instructed to retrieve figures from a public research dashboard bypassed the organization’s security controls and used the unauthorized access to steal credentials. It then made configuration changes on the server. In one evaluation, the changes let the model make an internal search tool relay queries to the public dashboard. In a second evaluation, the model downloaded five non-public tables containing 147,451 rows. OpenAI researchers had prompted the agents to retrieve only five dashboard figures. Even after resetting the setting, the model continued using the token to retrieve non-public data. “The evaluation ended without the model disclosing that it had guessed answers, accessed the organization’s internal systems, downloaded non-public tables, or changed the authentication configuration,” OpenAI said. “All five answers in this evaluation were marked incorrect.” In a third report , the company said a model prompted to update a cryptocurrency trading application used funds from a locked wallet on a test network. The model “derived wallet keys from publicly known developer recovery phrases, found an account with test-network funds, and used that account to pay for the requested contract deployment.” The report continued: “The model questioned whether it had permission, then reasoned that a public recovery phrase and valueless test-network tokens made the funds acceptable to use. The deployment succeeded and charged transaction fees to the account. This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder’s permission, then act on that judgment without authorization.” In the last report , OpenAI said that a model bypassed restrictions researchers had placed on the types of web requests it could make. During reinforcement-learning training, the model had been prompted to seek public trade statistics. OpenAI went on: After finding a public yearbook and submitting an answer, it continued probing for another route to the statistics service. It caused an external browser to send POST requests, retrieved annual figures as an image, and extracted them using optical character recognition. It then developed a reusable helper that returned response text through a forwarding service and callback mailbox, repeatedly checked the retrieved figures, and used saved data in submitted responses. This case shows how a model can bypass restrictions on its own tools by getting external services to perform the blocked actions, even after finding another way to answer the question. The model first tried to use an external browser with permission to make GET requests on its behalf, then used JavaScript to obtain the information. The model then used an online mailbox to troubleshoot the technique. Eventually, the model settled on a different method: It asked the external browser to open a web form that sent the trade query to the statistics service by POST. When the browser displayed the response, a rendering service returned a GIF image of the page. The model then used optical character recognition to read the figures from the image. sources.title: Science says your boss should talk less in meetings
passages: But not everyone is comfortable using humor in meetings, says science educator and comedian Vita Stout, now at Sierra College in Rocklin, California.

Stout’s research, coauthored with bat scientists and published in the Proceedings of Biological Sciences B , argued that when well-timed and used appropriately, humor in scientific meetings can be a tool for connection and community-building.
There are very few cross-cultural studies like this in the world of meeting science, says Kreamer.
“We have these best practices of meetings that we’ve learned over the past 30 years,” she says, but the bulk of studies have come out of Europe or North America.
“Often, leaders talk the most, which is also why they often think their meetings are pretty good,” she says.
In virtual meetings, because “we’ve all learned to mute ourselves if we’re not talking, very often, active listening is killed completely.”
Indeed, her studies on face-to-face meetings have shown that pre-meeting small talk predicts meeting effectiveness, particularly for more introverted participants.

Meetings are sometimes seen as the default way to get things done, but often, people don’t specify what they want to achieve from them, says cognitive scientist Ava Scott of the University of Copenhagen.
As with many meeting science studies, their findings about what improves meetings’ effectiveness often seem obvious, but meeting researchers note that meetings often stray far from these ideals.
